item.title: Airlines' new normal: Higher fares, fewer flights
item.description:
That wince you just made while researching travel options? Get used to it.

Why it matters: Soaring jet fuel prices are accelerating changes across the airline industry, seen in higher fares, premium-heavy cabins and fewer flight options for travelers.

  • Airfares rose 22% year over year in September, marking a 10th straight monthly increase in the government's airfare price index, which hit an all-time high.

State of play: All the major airlines are feeling the pain:

  • American Airlines reported Thursday that its fuel bill jumped nearly 70% in the third quarter from a year ago, adding $1.9 billion in costs and undercutting its revenue growth.
  • Southwest and United Airlines both slashed their profit forecasts this week on higher fuel costs.
  • And Delta Air Lines expects its fuel bill this year to come in $6 billion above last year's.

The impact: To protect their bottom lines, airlines are raising fares and turning to more premium seats to squeeze more revenue out of their flights.

  • At Southwest, the average passenger fare rose 26.9% to $231.69 in the third quarter, compared with a year earlier — and that doesn't include fees.
  • Delta's premium seating revenue jumped 18% in the third quarter, even though the number of premium seats rose only 6%.

What they're saying: The airlines have few options to make up for extra fuel costs other than fare increases, said Scott Keyes, founder of flight-deal service Going.com.

  • "None of them are hedging fuel the way they used to, in large part because they had a pretty terrible experience with it," Keyes said in an interview.

The big picture: Airline executives, however, see these changes — many of which were already underway — as a necessary new normal.

  • This year's fuel spike has only "accelerated" change, Delta CEO Ed Bastian said on the company's earnings call on Oct. 9.
  • "Regardless of the next move in fuel prices, the forces reshaping the U.S. airline industry will continue with many carriers struggling to earn their cost of capital well before the run-up in fuel," he said.
  • United CEO Scott Kirby told investors Wednesday that the industry's underlying costs — including airport fees, maintenance and engines — have increased so much in recent years that airlines must fundamentally change their economics.

Zoom in: Executives echoed Bastian's comments on pricing from earlier in the month, suggesting this week that the higher fares and other changes to protect profitability are likely to remain in place even after jet fuel prices ease.

  • "I'm pretty confident that we're not going to take steps backwards in pricing," Kirby said. "I think we're demonstrating this year that it's different this time."
  • American CEO Robert Isom said the fuel price spike "has just been a catalyst to allow us to realize that there is value," referring to the strong demand from customers willing to pay higher fares.

And airlines are becoming increasingly reluctant to operate flights that don't make money — potentially leaving travelers with fewer options.

  • United's Kirby predicted that trend will continue across the industry. "One golden rule — don't fly places that lose money," he said on the company's earnings call. "There's going to be less loss-making flying," he predicted.

Zoom out: The fallout from higher fuel prices — triggered largely by the war in Iran, which has throttled supplies — started with the shutdown of Spirit Airlines earlier this year.

  • While Spirit's troubles were many, the fuel price spike was widely seen as the last straw for the budget carrier.
  • And its exit means it's now easier for airlines to get away with charging more to cover their extra fuel costs, Keyes said.
  • "Spirit's demise is another factor in why you're seeing airfare go up so precipitously because they and other budget airlines act as something of an anchor for airfare in general," Keyes said.

The bottom line: Fuel prices may eventually come back down. Don't count on airfares following.

item.title: Judge curbs Trump administration's noncitizen voting probes
item.description:
A federal judge restricted Department of Homeland Security investigations into suspected noncitizen voting in nine states, citing concerns that the agency's tactics could intimidate eligible voters.

Why it matters: With the midterms less than two weeks away, the ruling curtails a central part of the Trump administration's efforts to investigate suspected noncitizen voting.

Driving the news: The ruling, issued late Wednesday, blocks election-related field operations and interviews under the government's Unlawful Voter Initiative that involve or are likely to involve U.S. citizens.

  • California-based U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín also blocked the administration from conducting operations against likely citizens in states relying on records generated by its voter-matching policy.

Zoom in: Martínez-Olguín wrote in her order that the groups that sued provided "substantial evidence" that the government's "intimidating conduct" was "directly interfering with their members' right to encourage voters to participate in the 2026 midterm elections."

  • Her order stated that DHS had compiled a "target list" of individuals from a variety of sources, including state voter rolls and commercial data.
  • But Martínez-Olguín cast doubt on the accuracy of the administration's data, warning of a "high likelihood of error in review because there is no federal database containing citizenship status of U.S. residents."
  • Court filings indicated that officers were ordered to prioritize probes in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.

Catch up quick: Democratic Sens. Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) and Alex Padilla (Calif.) released a whistleblower report last month alleging that officials had diverted fraud and national security personnel to the Unlawful Voter Initiative using "highly questionable data" and methods.

  • The whistleblower disclosure alleged that officers were directed, in violation of state law, to access sensitive voter information under minimal training and significant pressure.

The other side: "DHS is laser focused on identifying, prosecuting, and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens," a spokesperson told Axios in a statement, adding that the department has "no plans to question or investigate people we believe to be U.S. citizens."

  • Responding to the nonprofits and local government entities that sued, the administration argued in court that DHS "reasonably decided to make use of the best data it had available to it to perform its law enforcement role, notwithstanding that the information may not be perfect in all cases."
  • The administration also contended that the allegations of voter intimidation were too vague.
  • The White House referred Axios to DHS for comment.

Zoom out: Courts have repeatedly blocked the Trump administration's attempts to obtain state voter data, but the administration has pursued suspected noncitizen voting — which is rare — through other means.

  • Last week, the administration sued California and election officials over claims that suspected ineligible voters received mail-in ballots for the election, asking a court to delay about 20,000 voters from having their ballots counted.
  • But as Axios' Brittany Gibson notes, administration-created lists of potential noncitizens on voter rolls have been found less than accurate before, including in Nevada.

What we're watching: The administration faces continuing legal challenges to its election-related initiatives ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.

  • On Tuesday, Democratic groups sued the government, accusing it of using unfounded fraud claims as a cudgel to insert itself into election administration.

Go deeper: Trump's October barrage

A federal judge restricted Department of Homeland Security investigations into suspected noncitizen voting in nine states, citing concerns that the agency's tactics could intimidate eligible voters.

Why it matters: With the midterms less than two weeks away, the ruling curtails a central part of the Trump administration's efforts to investigate suspected noncitizen voting.

Driving the news: The ruling, issued late Wednesday, blocks election-related field operations and interviews under the government's Unlawful Voter Initiative that involve or are likely to involve U.S. citizens.

  • California-based U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín also blocked the administration from conducting operations against likely citizens in states relying on records generated by its voter-matching policy.

Zoom in: Martínez-Olguín wrote in her order that the groups that sued provided "substantial evidence" that the government's "intimidating conduct" was "directly interfering with their members' right to encourage voters to participate in the 2026 midterm elections."

  • Her order stated that DHS had compiled a "target list" of individuals from a variety of sources, including state voter rolls and commercial data.
  • But Martínez-Olguín cast doubt on the accuracy of the administration's data, warning of a "high likelihood of error in review because there is no federal database containing citizenship status of U.S. residents."

item.title: Trump ordered to sit for deposition in $10 billion BBC lawsuit
item.description:
A federal judge on Thursday ordered President Trump to sit for a deposition by Dec. 11 in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC over an edit of one of his speeches that the president's lawyers say was misleading.

Why it matters: The order will likely force Trump to answer questions under oath in a legal battle he started.

Driving the news: Judge Enjoliqué Lett ordered Trump to appear by Dec. 11, after lawyers for the BBC argued that Trump is improperly delaying his appearance.

  • In a filing published Wednesday, Trump's counsel said the president could appear between Jan. 11 and Jan. 22, 2027, and argued that his presidential duties prevent him from sitting for the deposition before then.
  • They also allege the BBC is "wrong to claim that President Trump is avoiding his deposition in this action."
  • The president was originally scheduled to appear for the deposition on Oct. 16. However, his lawyers said, that appearance was canceled because Trump had to attend to "matters that have significantly impacted the United States' national security and economy," including the wars in Iran and Ukraine and the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.

The other side: BBC attorneys say the president was campaigning in Georgia on Oct. 16, as reflected in a White House press pool report that includes his travel plans.

  • The BBC argues the president chose political activity over appearing for the original deposition date.
  • According to Trump's daily schedule, he attended an intelligence briefing and had executive time before departing for a rally in Georgia and then attended an RNC event in Palm Beach, Florida, that evening.

The White House referred Axios to Trump's personal counsel.

  • A spokesperson for Trump's legal team told Axios in an emailed statement that the BBC "defamed President Trump by intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring his speech in a brazen attempt to interfere in the 2024 Presidential Election."

The BBC's legal team did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment on the accusations Trump's legal team made in its statement.

  • When Axios perviously asked for comment, the BBC's attorneys told Axios they "have nothing to add."

Catch up quick: The defamation suit stems from a documentary the BBC aired that spliced together clips from Trump's speech on Jan. 6, 2021, the day of the riots at the U.S. Capitol.

  • The president claimed the edit was defamatory and demanded the BBC make amends by providing financial compensation, in addition to an apology and a retraction.
  • The BBC later said in a correction note that the clips "unintentionally created the impression that we were showing a single continuous section of the speech, rather than excerpts from different points in the speech, and that this gave the mistaken impression that President Trump had made a direct call for violent action."
  • Two top leaders at BBC later resigned over the backlash.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

item.title: Top health adviser and MAHA ally quits Trump admin
item.description:
Calley Means, the health entrepreneur who became the Trump administration's most vocal advocate of the MAHA agenda, resigned from his senior adviser post on Thursday.

Why it matters: Means' departure two weeks before the midterm elections underscores the MAHA base's discontent with the pace of change on food policy and the administration's stances on issues like pesticide use.

Driving the news: Means expressed "tremendous respect" for President Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in a statement on X, praising their efforts to take on "entrenched, dark forces in DC" and advance the MAHA agenda.

  • He cited the administration's work to overhaul dietary guidelines, advance psychedelic therapies, ban the use of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits for sugary drinks, and get food companies to voluntarily remove artificial dyes and other additives from products.
  • The Department of Health and Human Services didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Between the lines: Tensions between the MAHA faithful and the administration peaked in February, after Trump issued an executive order to increase domestic production of glyphosate, a common weed killer.

  • Kennedy and others close to the movement had argued pesticides are making Americans sick. But agriculture interests said restricting their use would raise food prices and cost farmers billions.

Trump had tapped Means' sister, Casey, a nutrition influencer, for surgeon general last year but withdrew the nomination in April after her confirmation process stalled in the Senate.

item.title: Black October: why bugs discovered by OpenAI tech are creating a cyber emergency
item.description:
The websites you use every day may have been vulnerable to hackers for years because of hidden flaws in their code that AI only recently discovered.

Why it matters: The code, called PHP, powers millions of websites, and the vulnerabilities could allow hackers to steal sensitive data like your passwords or take control of affected servers.

Driving the news: A potential attack exploiting flaws in PHP emerged on Wednesday, which prompted governments and companies to temporarily take their websites offline while they installed security patches.

  • Dozens of websites in the U.S., U.K., and around the world were briefly taken offline to make the fix.
  • The disruption put the National Security Agency and Europe's cybersecurity agency on alert.

State of play: Security patches were released to fix the issues on Oct. 21, 2026. Cybersecurity firms urged anyone using PHP to install the security updates immediately.

What they're saying: OpenAI's technology helped find the bugs, and the company called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory."

  • "To our knowledge, frontier AI found these vulnerabilities before attackers did," OpenAI said.
  • The cybersecurity firm Wiz wrote in a blog post: "These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history."

Read more below.

What is PHP?

You've probably never heard of PHP, even though you've interacted with it for decades.

  • PHP, which stands for Hypertext Preprocessor, is a programming language used by roughly 70% of websites whose server-side language is known.
  • It has been around since the 1990s to help build websites, taking data and generating content sent to a browser.
  • It's still used today for a variety of websites, including Wikipedia, WordPress blogs and shopping websites.

How it works: HTML determines what a website displays. PHP works behind the scenes to collect information and generate content.

What was the PHP vulnerability, exactly?

AI researchers discovered two critical vulnerabilities in PHP that could allow an attacker to take control of a website's server without having legitimate access to it.

  • Hackers could exploit the flaws, dubbed "php2shell" by cybersecurity firms, to steal information from those websites.

Between the lines: The flaws went undetected for more than a decade because exploiting them required complex technical work that AI helped researchers discover, per Wiz.

Why cybersecurity incidents are a big deal

Thought bubble via Axios' Bradley Olson: The PHP vulnerabilities are so serious that the NSA warned website operators to take their sites down if they didn't have enough time to patch the bug.

  • But the cybersecurity problems in recent days have extended far beyond that and include disruptions to developer platforms, data leaks on public schools, break-ins at public companies and more.
  • A major Axios scoop also revealed that banks are detecting unauthorized third-party agent access inside customer accounts, a problem they are racing to contain.

Cyber pros are calling the series of attacks "Black October" due to the sheer volume and the level of risk, although so far many organizations have mitigated the risk and avoided massive real-world harm.

  • While defenders and AI companies have warned for months that a season of cyber emergencies would imminently arrive, they have also been working to secure some of the obscure software that still underpins much of the modern internet ecosystem.

The bottom line: As attacks continue, experts have urged users to secure passwords, use a password manager and also to avoid panic.

  • As with any cyber emergency, the true barometer of harm is the extent to which damage seeps into the real world, as it has done with ransomware that took hospital software offline or a pipeline system that disrupted fuel supplies briefly on the East Coast.

item.title: Canada hit back at Trump tariffs. Now the U.S. alleges possible election interference.
item.description:
The U.S. Embassy in Canada accused Canadian leaders of "openly" describing plans to "influence American politics," doubling down on Ambassador Pete Hoekstra's claims of potential election interference.

Why it matters: The accusation further deteriorates Washington's relationship with its northern neighbor under President Trump's costly trade war that's put political pressure on Republicans.

  • Canada targeted its retaliatory tariffs on politically salient states and products ahead of the U.S. midterms.

Driving the news: The embassy cited Canada's targeted tariffs as part of the influence accusations laid out in a Wednesday fact sheet.

  • It cited remarks from Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, including an August press conference where she said Canada was "targeting products that will target states in the U.S."
  • She added, "we're being wise and strategic to put political pressure." Joly has echoed that message throughout the trade tensions.
  • The fact sheet also cited Joly's meeting with Democrats. She recently huddled with Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker.

What they're saying: Asked about the accusations during a news conference, Prime Minister Mark Carney said "all of our actions are in the interest of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy."

Zoom out: The fact sheet also singled out conservative Ontario Premier Doug Ford over a 2025 anti-tariff ad campaign featuring excerpts from a Ronald Reagan speech.

  • It also cited Liberal MP Anthony Housefather's campaigning for Florida Democrat Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz.
  • The memo read, "The Canadian government brushes off concerns about potential interference in U.S. elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances."

Catch up quick: Hoekstra said in a recent podcast interview that American officials were "closely watching" Canada for potential election interference.

  • Joly said last week it was "absolutely not" fair to characterize Canada's actions as election interference. Her visits, she said, were aimed to attract investments.
  • Carney, after cheering Canada's reduced dependence on the U.S. in a speech earlier this month, joked, "Careful, they might think that's election interference," seemingly a jab at Hoekstra.

Worth noting: The Trump administration has taken an increasingly antagonistic approach to Canada, from trade tensions to threats over its sovereignty.

  • In August, Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario, which straddles the U.S.-Canada border, to "Lake America."
  • He's also continuously said Canada should become the "51st state."

The big picture: Trump himself has openly weighed in on politics beyond U.S. borders, including during Canada's 2025 election campaign and ahead of Israel's elections this month.

  • On Sunday, Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection just nine days before Israel's national vote.

Go deeper: Escalated U.S.-Canada trade talks threaten fallout

item.title: Permitting deal draws lobbying blitz as hurdles mount
item.description:
The fragile Senate permitting deal is a major priority across the energy industry, per newly filed lobbying disclosures.

Why it matters: The filings reveal behind-the-scenes efforts by powerful interests and companies representing oil and gas, mining, renewables, environmentalists and plenty in between to shape the legislation.

The big picture: The bill title (Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act), its acronym (BAAJA) and its bill number appear throughout third-quarter lobbying disclosures.

  • The bill was introduced Sept. 30, the last day of the third quarter. The disclosures, due Oct. 20, offer a window into efforts to influence the legislation during its drafting and negotiations.
  • The lobbying extends beyond groups that specifically named the bill in their filings. Many others with a stake in the bill — like the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Manufacturers — list permitting legislation in other ways.

Driving the news: Here's just a small subset of the parties in the arena.

  • Industry groups like the American Petroleum Institute, the Edison Electric Institute, the American Forest & Paper Association, the National Mining Association, and the Data Center Coalition.
  • Green groups including Earthjustice, the Nature Conservancy, and Defenders of Wildlife.
  • Low-carbon power trade groups such as the Solar Energy Industries Association.

State of play: The lobbying goes far beyond trade associations, with many individual companies also involved.

  • They range from Chevron and BP to power giants like Duke Energy and Southern Company to geothermal startup Fervo.
  • Industrial and equipment heavyweights like Caterpillar, Schneider Electric and Cummins are there, too.

Zoom in: The disclosures also offer clues about which provisions attracted lobbying attention. For example:

  • The National Mining Association identified BAAJA provisions that would change Clean Water Act permitting, including state water quality reviews and limits on lawsuits challenging permits.
  • The Interstate Natural Gas Association of America listed BAAJA provisions affecting interstate natural gas pipelines among its lobbying topics, alongside other pipeline permitting proposals.

Threat level: The latest filings land amid new friction over the bill.

  • This week the Interior Department asked a federal judge to allow it to reconsider the Biden-era prior approval of Avangrid's planned New England Wind project off Massachusetts.
  • "This is how you blow up a permitting deal," Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) told Axios and other outlets about the latest in a string of Trump team moves against previously approved projects.

Yes, but: An administration official cast the federal filing as a procedural move in the case brought by other opponents of the project.

  • "Our filings defend the current government's litigating position," the official said.
  • "We have been very transparent about the need for permitting reform and have also been transparent with Senator Whitehouse's and Senator [Martin] Heinrich's teams on all these legal filings," the official said, citing the two Democratic co-authors.

🆕 The latest: Democratic attorneys general from nine states express "substantial concerns" with the bill in a new letter to lawmakers, Punchbowl News reported this morning.

What we're watching: The public advocacy and closed-door maneuvering should reach a fever pitch ahead of the first procedural vote on Nov. 9, and in the days and weeks that follow.

  • The next wave of disclosures, covering October-December, should provide an even clearer look at the interests at play.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: Young Americans are losing faith in the future — and Trump
item.description:
Data: Harvard Youth Poll, Fall 2026; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios

Nearly two in three U.S. adults younger than 30 who plan to vote in next month's congressional midterm elections say their main motivation is to oppose President Trump and his policies, according to a newly released Harvard Youth Poll.

The big picture: Seventy-seven percent of respondents disapprove of the president's handling of the economy, including about half of young Republicans. And just 9% say the U.S. is headed in the right direction — the lowest in the survey's history.

Why it matters: Economic populism is driving emotions, along with concerns about war, AI, billionaires, deportation tactics, social policies and corruption. Majorities of respondents support Medicare for All, a wealth tax and bans on congressional stock trading.

What we're watching: Just one in three Americans ages 18-29 say they'll definitely vote — a substantial drop from 40% who said so in 2022. Notably, most of that drop is driven by Republicans.

  • Only 34% of Republican respondents said they'll definitely vote, down from 46%; 50% of young Democrats say they'll definitely vote, essentially unchanged. Just 22% of independents they'll definitely vote, down from 26%.
Data: Harvard Youth Poll; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios

Zoom in: Topping the list of what young people consider serious threats to their long-term financial security: rising prices and the cost of living (79%), followed by the power of large corporations (68%) and trade wars (68%).

  • Nearly half said their household is struggling to make ends meet or getting by with limited financial security.

By the numbers: 63% say their votes for U.S. House or Senate will be cast in opposition to Trump, while 14% say they're motivated by support of the president and 17% say he's not a factor.

  • Two-thirds disapprove of the job Democrats are doing in Congress; 74% disapprove of congressional Republicans' performance.

Stunning stats: For the first time in the poll's history, the share of young adults who said they expect to be worse off than their parents (27%) slightly exceeded the share who said they expect to be better off (25%).

  • The difference was within the poll's margin of error, but the longer-term trend is striking. In fall 2021, 39% expected to be better off than their parents, while just 17% expected to be worse off.
  • When Harvard first asked the question, only to college students, in 2003, 74% believed they'd be better off than their parents. In this recent poll only 28% believed it.
  • When asked if they're more hopeful or fearful about America's future, fear (69%) outweighs hope (26%) by more than two to one.

What they're saying: "At the beginning of adulthood, younger people should be able to see a path from hard work to a secure life, and the big question is whether that promise still holds," John Della Volpe, director of polling at Harvard Kennedy School's Institute of Politics, said in a conference call with reporters Wednesday.

Methodology: The Harvard Youth Poll was conducted Sept. 30-Oct. 7, 2026, by the Harvard Public Opinion Project (HPOP) with Ipsos' KnowledgePanel®. It is based on a probability-based sample of 2,024 18-to-29-year-olds.

  • The margin of sampling error is +/-2.61% for results based on the entire sample of adults; +/- 3.19% for the sample of registered voters; and +/-4.30% for the sample of those who plan to "definitely" or are likely to vote.

item.title: Hackers are turning web browsing into a spyware trap
item.description:
Hackers are finding new ways to infect iPhones with spyware — even when victims never click a malicious link — according to new research shared with Axios.

Why it matters: Software once used to spy on politicians, journalists and other high-value targets is becoming a tool for everyday cybercriminals looking to steal cryptocurrency and login credentials.

Driving the news: Researchers at iVerify and Report URI said Thursday they've uncovered two campaigns in which criminal groups with suspected ties to China exploited online advertising infrastructure and legitimate websites to deliver iPhone spyware.

  • In one case, iVerify found that a financial institution employee's iPhone was infected after they scrolled past a professional soccer advertisement on Instagram. The ad automatically triggered an attack that stole the person's login credentials and searched their cryptocurrency wallets.
  • In another, Report URI uncovered a campaign affecting nearly 8,000 legitimate websites after hackers purchased roughly 630 expired domains that those sites still relied on. The attackers used those domains to redirect vulnerable iPhone visitors toward spyware designed to steal their credentials and cryptocurrency.

How it works: Both campaigns exploited tools that load automatically as people browse the internet, eliminating the need to trick victims into clicking malicious links.

  • In the iVerify case, malicious code began running as soon as the Instagram advertisement appeared on the victim's screen. The attack checked the iPhone's operating system before deploying a compatible exploit.
  • In the Report URI campaign, attackers purchased expired domains once used to host legitimate website features, such as chatbots and analytics tools. Thousands of websites were still loading code from those domains, allowing criminals to quietly redirect visitors toward malicious software.

Threat level: The findings show how cybercriminals are building an infrastructure for delivering spyware through everyday online activity, rather than relying on traditional phishing attacks or targeting specific individuals.

  • Both methods also allow attackers to selectively target vulnerable devices. Advertising platforms can narrow audiences based on interests and device characteristics, while malicious website code can identify a visitor's operating system before selecting an attack.

The big picture: Cybercriminals are increasingly weaponizing spyware to exploit mobile phones, whose security (whether on an iPhone or Android) has often been seen as ironclad.

  • Last year, iVerify uncovered evidence of the first spyware campaign targeting iPhones in the U.S. and the European Union.
  • Last week, researchers at the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab uncovered the first public confirmation of zero-click spyware delivered via targeted ads — targeting at least 45 devices within international news network Al Jazeera.
  • Rocky Cole, co-founder and chief operating officer at iVerify, told Axios that spyware is now "the fastest proliferating threat to mobile devices at the current moment."

The intrigue: "They're either Chinese or they definitely want us to think that they are," Scott Helme, founder and CEO at Report URI, told Axios about the groups behind the campaigns.

What to watch: Researchers warn that the growing availability of sophisticated spyware is forcing consumers to rethink how they protect their phones.

  • Cole and Helme both emphasized keeping mobile operating systems updated, since the attacks depend on exploiting vulnerabilities in specific software versions.

item.title: "Stop whining": What Vance's take on Ohio ad controversy means for 2028
item.description:
Vice President Vance's call for fellow Republicans to "stop whining" about Vivek Ramaswamy's controversial attack ad in Ohio's race for governor showed a key part of his political mindset ahead of his expected run for president in 2028: Never back down.

Why it matters: Channeling President Trump, Vance has shown contempt for what he sees as the old-guard GOP's reflex to cave under pressure from Democrats and the media.

  • He thinks too many Republicans sacrifice allies to make controversies go away, and that giving critics a political scalp only encourages them to demand another, according to people familiar with his thinking.
  • It's an approach with some risk — namely whether Vance, entering a critical period in his political career, has the political muscle to get away with Trump's no-apologies approach.

Driving the news: Vance on Wednesday defended Ramaswamy amid bipartisan outrage over an ad featuring the estranged mother of Ramaswamy's Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.

  • In the deeply personal ad, Acton's mother calls her daughter a liar, and says Ohioans shouldn't vote for her for governor.
  • Not mentioned in the ad: Acton and her brother were removed from the mother's care as children after Acton accused her stepfather of sexual abuse. Her mother sided with the stepfather, leading to an estrangement that has lasted nearly 50 years.

Appearing at a campaign stop for Ramaswamy in Ohio, Vance showed little concern about the criticism over the ad.

  • Vance said he was "disgusted" by fellow Republicans criticizing it, telling them to "stop whining."
  • Asked whether the ad was appropriate, Vance said it was "not really my concern," and that politics is tough.

The other side: The backlash has included Republicans and Democrats who believe the ad crossed a moral line by exploiting Acton's traumatic childhood.

  • "I would not have run that ad," Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, who appeared alongside Vance and Ramaswamy at a campaign rally Wednesday, told the AP.
  • Former UN ambassador Nikki Haley called Ramaswamy "a bad guy," adding: "It's a shame he continues to get away with it."

Acton told CNN that she hopes her story of recovering from abuse inspires others, and that she "was not stunned" at "the antics of an out-of-touch billionaire," referring to Ramaswamy.

Behind the scenes: Vance's refusal to denounce allies dates to his 2022 Senate campaign in Ohio.

  • During a March 2022 debate, Vance refused to condemn then-Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) for appearing at a rally organized by white nationalist Nick Fuentes. "She is my friend, and she did nothing wrong ... I'm absolutely not gonna throw her under the bus," Vance said then.
  • In the final days of Ohio's 2024 Senate primary, Vance aggressively defended GOP candidate Bernie Moreno amid a controversy over an adult dating website account linked to Moreno's work email.

As vice president, Vance has refused to disavow his friend Tucker Carlson amid accusations of antisemitism — even as Carlson's relationship with Trump was fracturing.

  • After racist and antisemitic messages surfaced in a leaked Young Republicans group chat, Vance declared on X that he wouldn't join the "pearl clutching."
  • During a December 2025 speech at a Turning Point USA event, Vance rejected political "purity tests," declaring: "I didn't bring a list of conservatives to denounce or to de-platform."

What they're saying: "There is nothing JD has more personal disdain for than weak Republicans who reflexively kowtow every time the Dem-media demands a scalp," a source close to Vance told Axios.

  • "It drives him crazy to see the cucked reaction from some establishment operatives and politicians in the GOP, who he views as nothing more than useful idiots for the left."

The intrigue: Some Republicans see Vance as influenced by Trump and Vance's mentor, tech billionaire Peter Thiel, who has embraced a similar no-apologies mantra.

  • "The president's refusal to kowtow to the left is one of the things JD admires most" about Trump, the Vance source said.

item.title: Scoop: Unvetted AI agents are accessing U.S. bank accounts
item.description:
Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, with some agents attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources tell Axios.

Why it matters: AI agents are becoming a nightmare for America's banks, making their way into banking systems faster than financial institutions can respond.

  • The difficulty in distinguishing between a human and an unauthorized bot is forcing banks to block the technology and rapidly rewrite their terms of service.

Driving the news: Banks including Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and others are racing to contain agent risks. Some are aware of unauthorized access, people familiar with the issue said.

  • These are generally situations when an agent or AI assistant accesses a human's account with the user's permission and login credentials. Even if permitted by the user, this goes against the guidelines of most banks requiring that humans log in to their own accounts.
  • This presents significant security risks: Banking executives fear the steps agents with login access might take, especially if a user has granted purchase authority or the ability to shift funds.
  • In other instances, some banks have tracked activity when agents — programmed to fulfill requests or complete tasks on a user's behalf — contact call centers or appear to take actions independent of user instructions, the people said.

What they're saying: Bank executives described the situation as horrifying, with one official saying the industry has grave concerns about agents gaining access to customer accounts and taking steps that could impact user finances.

State of play: The concerns are at the root of the decision by several banks to restrict third-party AI agent access, the people said.

  • Morgan Stanley has begun blocking third-party agents from accessing its platforms, sources familiar with the decision said.
  • JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi are also restricting agents.
  • A Chase spokesperson said customers should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone. A Morgan Stanley spokesperson said the bank hasn't observed instances of "rogue AI agents accessing our platforms."

Zoom out: Most banks have authorized or are moving in the direction of allowing read-only access, which should allow agents to see customer financial information without taking action.

  • Banks already grant such access to third-party apps like Quicken for budgeting and other activities.

Reality check: Several industry and bank executives told Axios they recognize the need to find a middle-ground with AI agents.

  • Customers will want to use these agents going forward, which banks recognize.
  • But for now, the risks of being too permissive are too high.

Threat level: Many banks are broadly not able to parse whether agent account activity is user-directed, sources said.

  • One bank executive told Axios they struggle to differentiate between agents, as well as whether an agent has been authorized by a user or has gone rogue and gained access to a customer account.

What we're watching: On one hand, banks are best positioned to respond to the threats and opportunities of AI given their cash on hand and experience as critical infrastructure.

  • But money isn't necessarily enough to solve this problem, one source said, because of how quickly the technology is developing and revealing new weaknesses in real time.
  • Banks are investing in preventing worst-case scenarios, but they are also preparing in case they do happen, including with "day after" scenario planning that would allow them to quickly secure or restore customer access, sources said.

The bottom line: The rapid pace of AI advancement is becoming a security nightmare for America's financial institutions.

item.title: Democrats accuse Trump of using prosecution threats to pressure election officials
item.description:
Democratic groups sued the Trump administration Tuesday, accusing it of using unfounded voter fraud claims to muscle its way into how states run elections.

Why it matters: The groups say the administration is issuing a stream of threats to intimidate and bully both voters and election officials.

  • They're asking a judge to declare the administration's actions unlawful and block further interference.

Driving the news: The lawsuit condemns the administration for targeting state voter rolls by insisting that local officials review federally compiled lists of alleged noncitizens on their voter rolls.

  • The suit also alleges that the administration is improperly demanding that states deny ballots to registered voters based on those federal lists.
  • The Democrat-aligned groups also claim the administration has attempted to intimidate state and local officials by threatening them with jail time or prosecution.

Case in point: The lawsuit cites a Department of Homeland Security claim that Nevada had nearly 16,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls.

  • The department later claimed that it had confirmed 185 of those people were noncitizens. State records later indicated that all 185 were citizens.
  • The DOJ also demanded that California deny ballots to more than 20,000 people based on a federal list that flagged them as suspected ineligible voters, the lawsuit says.
  • A preliminary investigation by Los Angeles County investigators found that more than 25% of those flagged listed a U.S. birthplace, and others already had their voter registrations canceled.

What they're saying: "Department of Justice and DHS officials have sought to bolster their interference efforts through a persistent stream of threats and intimidation directed towards state and local election officials across the country," the groups' attorneys wrote.

  • "Defendants' coercive threats of legal retaliation against state officials, including even potential imprisonment, for simply following state law and aiding registered voters in casting their ballots objectively intimidate voters and election officials alike, in violation of Section 11(b) of the Voting Rights Act."
  • The suit, brought by Democratic organizations including the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, Democratic leaders and a voter, names Trump, the Departments of Justice and Homeland Security, and their respective heads as defendants.

The other side: "The Justice Department enforces federal election law, and election integrity is a top priority," a DOJ spokesperson told Axios.

  • "Every action the Department has taken to protect the integrity of this year's elections is grounded in the law and being litigated in open court. Ensuring that only eligible citizens vote and that every lawful ballot is counted is a requirement of federal law," according to the emailed statement.
  • "We notified California that noncitizens are likely registered to vote, and we asked the state to independently verify the citizenship of any ballots cast by people on a list that we provided. It refused to do so. Federal law doesn't permit this willful blindness."

A White House spokesperson told Axios that while "Democrats and the media continue to dismiss concerns about voter fraud, the Trump Administration is taking decisive lawful action to protect our elections including prosecuting election crimes, strengthening election infrastructure security, and protecting vulnerable voters from fraud and coercion."

  • A spokesperson for Homeland Security told Axios that the department's "message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation."

Zoom out: The suit also argues that the president has no constitutional authority to decide who gets to vote or dictate how states count ballots.

  • Investigations and audits have found no evidence of widespread voter fraud. Research shows noncitizen voting is rare, and there's no evidence it occurs on a scale that could swing elections.

Go deeper: Trump sues California to prevent counting 20,000 voters' ballots

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from the White House and DHS.

The other side: "The Justice Department enforces federal election law, and election integrity is a top priority," a DOJ spokesperson told Axios.

  • "Every action the Department has taken to protect the integrity of this year's elections is grounded in the law and being litigated in open court. Ensuring that only eligible citizens vote and that every lawful ballot is counted is a requirement of federal law," according to the emailed statement.
  • "We notified California that noncitizens are likely registered to vote, and we asked the state to independently verify the citizenship of any ballots cast by people on a list that we provided. It refused to do so. Federal law doesn't permit this willful blindness."

A White House spokesperson told Axios that while "Democrats and the media continue to dismiss concerns about voter fraud, the Trump Administration is taking decisive lawful action to protect our elections including prosecuting election crimes, strengthening election infrastructure security, and protecting vulnerable voters from fraud and coercion."

  • A spokesperson for Homeland Security told Axios that the department's "message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation."

Zoom out: The suit also argues that the president has no constitutional authority to decide who gets to vote or dictate how states count ballots.

  • Investigations and audits have found no evidence of widespread voter fraud. Research shows noncitizen voting is rare, and there's no evidence it occurs on a scale that could swing elections.

Go deeper: Trump sues California to prevent counting 20,000 voters' ballots

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from the White House and DHS.

item.title: Scoop: Dems quietly guide super PACs to boost spoiler House candidates
item.description:
House Democrats' campaign arm is instructing allied super PACs to promote minor candidates in several key House races, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: This allows Democrats to steer outside groups toward siphoning votes from Republicans without violating laws against direct coordination.

  • An Axios review of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee's "redboxes" — publicly available webpages laying out what PACs should say in ads and which voters to target — found references to minor candidates in five races.
  • The DCCC included language on four of those pages promoting a third-party or independent candidate with language touting their conservative, pro-gun or anti-government bona fides.

"Registered Republicans under the age of 55 need to see ads," the redbox for Colorado's 5th District says, "showing that ... Christopher Mitchell, a libertarian, is the true conservative running for Congress."

  • The page for Virginia's 2nd District says white, college-educated men should see that independent J. Matt Baker is "a staunch supporter of the 2nd amendment" who will "defend our constitution."
  • In Virginia's 5th District, the DCCC wants the same group of voters to know that independent Cooke Harvey "will fight for Virginia's farmers against big government."
  • Republican women in Nevada's 2nd District should be informed that American Independent Party candidate Lynn Chapman "has spent decades fighting for conservative values," the DCCC says.

Zoom in: In several cases, the redboxes urge super PACs to steer Democratic and left-leaning voters away from minor candidates who could siphon votes from the DCCC's recruit.

  • The redbox for Alaska's at-large district — where Democrats are backing independent Bill Hill — says voters need to know Eric Hafner is a "fake Democrat" despite being listed on the ballot as one, noting he is an inmate in New York with no clear ties to Alaska.
  • The page for Virginia's 2nd District urges PACs to ding the progressive credentials of another independent candidate, Geral D. "Bishop" Staten, a self-identified "Democrat Socialist."
  • Black voters should hear that Staten "said that he would vote for Donald Trump in 2024 and said that President Obama is a quote 'puppet and a clown,'" the DCCC redbox says — though he has denied supporting Trump.

Between the lines: In the post-Citizens United era, redboxes have emerged as a way for campaigns to give messaging guidance to cash-rich outside groups that often have less localized knowledge of their turf.

  • The practice is so named because the websites often put a red box around the instructions.
  • The NRCC has its own publicly available redboxes, though it shies away from encouraging PACs to boost spoiler candidates.

The big picture: There have been several other isolated examples this year of both parties allegedly boosting spoiler candidates, including with redboxes.

  • Democrats successfully sued last month to get a Green Party candidate who they alleged was a GOP plant booted off the ballot in Pennsylvania's 7th District.
  • Republicans in Alaska tried and failed to do the same with unaffiliated candidate Dan J. Sullivan, who they allege is a spoiler for Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in his race against Democrat Mary Peltola.
  • It's even happened in party primaries: The campaign of Rep. Doris Matsui (D-Calif.) put language on its redbox promoting Republican Zachariah Wooden in the hopes of keeping progressive challenger Mai Vang out of the general election.

item.title: White House to Politico: Retract stories or face "consequences"
item.description:
The White House counsel's office warned Politico in a Monday letter that it had 48 hours to retract or correct recent stories about alleged staff drama, or it would suffer unspecified consequences.

  • That deadline expires Thursday.

Why it matters: The White House demand threatens to escalate already tense relations with Politico specifically and, more generally, the press corps that covers President Trump in Washington.

  • Politico, CNN, and MS NOW are already banned from covering Trump in the Oval Office and on Air Force One because the president does not like their coverage.
  • Trump blocked all three outlets from the White House grounds as well, but a judge on Oct. 13 restored their access.
  • CNN threatened legal action Wednesday to regain access to Air Force One and the "pool" of television networks that accompany the president.

Zoom in: In his letter to Politico, White House Counsel Will Scharf singled out three stories concerning White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles despite "on-the-record refutations" or contrary evidence supplied by senior staff and even the president.

  1. Oct. 15: In a story headlined "Trump's ice maiden is under fire," Politico Playbook reported that Trump was considering a replacement for Wiles. Trump called it "fake news."
  2. Oct. 16: Politico Playbook wrote that the prior day's story had caused a "freakout" and that the president "blew up" over it. A White House spokesman called it "unbelievably stupid and false."
  3. Oct. 16: In a story headlined "Susie Wiles helped set up Fox interview ahead of press secretary's exit," Politico insinuated the chief of staff set up Katie Zacharia to fail in a Sean Hannity interview on Fox the night before.
  • The White House and Fox News denied the reporting. And White House officials provided text messages to Politico before publication showing Zacharia — not Wiles — set up the interview, which the New York Post reported the following day.
  • "Politico has not corrected or retracted its false reporting. Instead, a Politico reporter confirmed that Politico declined to remove Ms. Wiles from the story because she was the 'hook' for the story — a legally fraught and alarming admission to say the least," Scharf wrote.

What they're saying: Scharf wrote that "freedom of the press is not a professional exemption from accountability. I therefore demand that Politico immediately correct or retract these publications, issue a prominent and public apology to the President of the United States and to Ms. Wiles, and remove the false reporting from your digital archives."

  • Otherwise, he wrote, the White House would conduct an "immediate review of Politico's relationship with the White House, and, of course, consideration of all other appropriate and available legal remedies."
  • A Politico spokesperson did not return a message seeking comment.
  • White House officials fault the new management at Politico for pushing its reporters to engage in what Scharf called "gossip-peddling."
  • The letter was addressed to global editor in chief Jonathan Greenberger.

Zoom out: Trump has had an ongoing love-hate relationship with the press. He is available to reporters for far more question-and-answer sessions than any recent president, but he's quick to anger and threaten press bans for coverage he doesn't like.

  • Early in his second term, Trump banned the Associated Press from the Oval Office and Air Force One access after it balked at calling the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. A federal judge reinstated AP's access months later.
  • The New York Times reported this week that Trump has mused about removing the press entirely from the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room and building a swimming pool there.

What's next: Scharf would not specify what consequences Politico faces, but a White House official said "all options are on the table" and described Trump's counsel as "uncharacteristically enraged."

  • Trump is highly litigious with media organizations and, advisers say, his appetite for launching lawsuits hasn't diminished.
  • Some advisers outside of the Trump White House noticed that administration officials may be telegraphing another avenue to attack Politico as a malign foreign influence because it's owned by a German company, Axel Springer.
  • "Politico is a foreign-op designed to interfere in American politics and meddle in our elections with disinformation and misinformation," White House Communications Director Steven Cheung wrote on X Saturday.

item.title: AI uncovers massive flaw in web's foundational code
item.description:
Security officials are sounding the alarm over two critical vulnerabilities in a programming language used to run millions of websites, marking one of the most consequential cybersecurity discoveries yet made with AI.

Why it matters: The bugs, which researchers found partly with an OpenAI model, proves AI can uncover critical flaws humans missed for decades — raising the stakes for defenders racing to fix vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them at machine speed.

What they're saying: Matthew Prince, the CEO of Cloudflare, a global connectivity and internet security company, said the company saw thousands of attempts to exploit the flaws in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced.

  • "That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now," he wrote on X.

Driving the news: There are two problems hackers could easily exploit in an open-source programming language known as PHP that's used on nearly 70% of all websites.

  • Government officials from the U.S. to Japan are warning companies to apply a patch to fix the bugs, or consider taking down their sites to avoid an attack.
  • OpenAI touted the role its model played in discovering one of the vulnerabilities, which allowed PHP researchers to create a fix.

Between the lines: Security researchers have been skeptical of AI-generated vulnerability reports, many of which have turned out to be minor bugs or false alarms.

  • But the PHP discovery could force the cybersecurity community to reckon with the reality of AI threats.
  • "It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post Wednesday.

Threat level: If exploited, the PHP flaws would allow malicious hackers to take control of vulnerable web servers without needing a password or other credentials.

  • Since PHP runs under a wide variety of internet applications, that access could allow hackers to take over websites, steal sensitive information and tamper with a website.
  • Some website owners took their sites down earlier Wednesday, including certain services at Wikipedia and 4chan, until they had time to patch their systems.
  • "These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history," researchers at Wiz wrote in a post.

The big picture: AI-driven bug discoveries are shining a light on the fragility of the modern internet, which is heavily reliant on a slew of open-source software powered by volunteers.

  • The two flaws in PHP existed for decades, but demonstrated that it was possible for a hacker to exploit them required "an exceptionally complex chain of steps," researchers at Wiz added.
  • "Defenders have always relied on the gap between 'vulnerable' and 'exploitable' to buy time to patch," Michael Leland, field CTO at Island, said in an email to Axios. "That gap is rapidly closing."

What we're watching: Cybersecurity defenders are on guard for what could be a wave of incidents where websites and organizations are hacked using these two vulnerabilities in the next few weeks.

Go deeper: Rogue AI agents expose internet's frail foundation

item.title: Scoop: Senate Republicans fear Mississippi is in play
item.description:
Senate Republicans are weighing three last-ditch spending moves that would have been unimaginable six months ago: a cash infusion for Mississippi and even more money for South Carolina and Kansas.

Why it matters: It's been 94 years since Kansas elected a Democratic senator, 44 years for Mississippi and 28 for South Carolina. But panic is spreading through the Republican Party.

  • "The wall has broken. The enemy is inside the fort," one national Republican political operative told Axios. "We are now fighting hand to hand."
  • The Senate map, which once looked impregnable for Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), is now full of vulnerabilities.
  • Democratic challengers are polling within the margin of error in more than half a dozen deep-red states, according to internal GOP polls.

The other side: "We're nervous about Alaska. We're nervous about Michigan. We're still going to hold the Senate at the end," said another operative.

Zoom in: Two weeks ago, when Senate Leadership Fund decided to take out a $5 million "insurance policy" in South Carolina, operatives took a hard look at Idaho, South Dakota and Mississippi.

  • At the time, they concluded they didn't need to spend any money in those states, according to a person familiar with the matter.
  • But Senate Republicans are now reviewing the Mississippi race and may need to spend there to protect Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith from a surprisingly competitive bid by Democratic district attorney Scott Colom.
  • Senate Majority PAC, the main super PAC for Senate Democrats, announced a $1.2 million investment in the race on Tuesday.

Zoom out: In early June, SLF started to reinforce a Midwestern red wall to protect the GOP majority, reserving $28 million in TV advertising in Ohio and $11 million in Iowa.

  • Those investments have ballooned to $93 million in Ohio and $53 million in Iowa.
  • After an initial $5 million buy in South Carolina, SLF's spending has increased to $8.5 million, according to AdImpact. And a super PAC linked to Sen. John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) is spending another $500,000 in South Carolina.
  • SLF, which is linked to Senate GOP leadership, has earmarked $14 million for Kansas, and has spent nearly $12 million there so far.
  • "No Republican seat is safe this cycle," another operative told Axios.

What we're hearing: Some GOP Senate candidates do, in fact, appear safe this cycle.

  • Republicans aren't overly concerned about Sens. Ashley Moody in Florida or Mike Rounds in South Dakota.

The intrigue: The National Republican Senatorial Committee raised $31.4 million last month, but its coffers appear to be drained. It took out a $20 million loan as it spends aggressively on its coordinated campaign strategy.

  • SLF ended September with $155 million in cash on hand, according to its FEC filing.
  • The group has spent or reserved $169 million worth of video ads since Oct. 1, according to AdImpact.
  • Even President Trump promised to unload another $100 million before Election Day in a Tuesday post on Truth Social, bringing the total from his super PACs to $400 million.

The bottom line: Republicans can still maintain their Senate majority, but none of the polling is giving them a great deal of confidence that they will do so.

item.title: Meta hit with $25 billion penalty for misleading Facebook users
item.description:
A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties Wednesday after a jury found in September that the social media giant misled users about their data privacy.

Why it matters: The penalties come nearly a decade after the Cambridge Analytica scandal first broke and signal that Big Tech can face significant financial consequences for misleading users about their privacy.

Driving the news: Judge Francis Mathew determined the penalty amount Wednesday, handing New Mexico a win as the only state to take its claims to trial after 48 others settled.

  • Mathew concluded New Mexico was entitled to $219.5 billion based on the state's maximum $5,000 penalty multiplied by 43,899,720 violations. He reduced that to $25 billion.

What they're saying: "This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," C.J. Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, told Axios in an emailed statement.

  • "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal. In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge."

Catch up quick: In September, a New Mexico jury said Meta had committed 43 million "willful violations" of the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act.

  • Mathew found that Facebook's privacy controls failed to give users meaningful control over their data and that third-party app developers could access their information through the platform's systems.
  • Mathew found Mark Zuckerberg knew users didn't understand how data privacy works, and exploited that, noting that the CEO had once written that users "probably don't understand their current privacy settings or care about who sees their updates."
  • Zuckerberg also wrote that the company should give users "a chance to change their privacy settings but obviously don't encourage it."

Zoom out: The suit followed reporting that revealed data firm Cambridge Analytica had harvested data from more than 50 million Facebook users to craft political ads during the 2016 election.

  • After the scandal, Facebook promised more transparency, but the court found Meta failed to consistently inform users when their data was misused.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.

  • Mathew found Mark Zuckerberg knew users didn't understand how data privacy works, and exploited that, noting that the CEO had once written that users "probably don't understand their current privacy settings or care about who sees their updates."
  • Zuckerberg also wrote that the company should give users "a chance to change their privacy settings but obviously don't encourage it."

Zoom out: The suit followed reporting that revealed data firm Cambridge Analytica had harvested data from more than 50 million Facebook users to craft political ads during the 2016 election.

  • After the scandal, Facebook promised more transparency, but the court found Meta failed to consistently inform users when their data was misused.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.

item.title: Israeli military conducts massive "power projection" operation near Iran's border
item.description:
Dozens of Israeli Air Force fighter jets conducted a sortie on Monday, flying as far as the Iranian border, according to Israeli and U.S. officials.

Why it matters: The operation, more than 800 miles away from Israel, took place a week before the Israeli elections and on the same day Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at Israel's Ovda Air Base. The sortie wasn't connected to Hegseth's visit.

  • While some Israeli and U.S. officials said the sortie wasn't unusual and that it was meant to deter Iran, it could have led to a miscalculation, triggering an Iranian response and reigniting the war.

Behind the scenes: The exercise involved dozens of fighter jets and refueling aircraft, the sources said.

  • It followed a flight path consistent with a potential strike against Iran, passing through Syrian and Iraqi airspace.
  • As the aircraft approached the Iranian border, they turned around and returned to Israel, the sources said.

The intrigue: U.S. officials said the Israelis knew that Iran's air defense systems would detect the sortie.

  • According to the sources, Israel notified the U.S. in advance and described the operation as a training exercise intended for "power projection" and aimed at deterring Iran from launching attacks against Israel ahead of the elections.
  • However, some U.S. sources said they had the impression that Israel was hoping the Iranians would fire at the aircraft, providing a justification for launching strikes against Iran.
  • Fox News reported on Tuesday that the Israeli Air Force conducted a drill towards Iran.

Driving the news: Last week, Axios reported that Netanyahu and President Trump discussed in early October the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections.

  • Netanyahu told Trump he was concerned about Israeli intelligence indicating Iran was taking troubling steps to reconstitute its nuclear program.
  • Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir told Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine at the time that restarting the war in that timeframe could cause the Israeli elections to be postponed, given that Iran would probably retaliate, the sources said.
  • Trump initially seemed to be inclined to resume attacks, but then grew hesitant and eventually decided against Netanyahu's proposal.

State of play: An Israeli official said Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir will not allow any unjustified military activity that could undermine the Oct. 27 elections.

What he's saying: On Wednesday Netanyahu said at a military graduation ceremony that Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei "has decided to follow in his father's footsteps" and allowed Iranian scientists to move forward with building a nuclear weapon.

  • "He has taken the safety off, and Iran is once again trying to develop its bombs of death," Netanyahu said.
  • "Therefore, there is only one way to eliminate this threat once and for all: to overthrow the regime in Iran. And that is the directive I have given to the IDF, the Mossad and the security agencies," he added.

item.title: The oil market's 2027 relief hopes are fading fast
item.description:
Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

Traders are betting that oil prices will remain elevated for longer than they anticipated just weeks ago, threatening to prolong the inflationary pressures that businesses and consumers have weathered for months.

Why it matters: Oil inventories have helped cushion the blow from disrupted Middle Eastern supplies, but much of that buffer has been depleted since the war began.

  • The possibility of sustained price pressures into next year throws into doubt the logic that central banks traditionally rely upon to look through energy price shifts — that they represent a one-time shift in relative prices, not an ongoing inflationary process.
  • That leaves the global economy more vulnerable to another energy price surge, with potentially more lasting consequences for growth, inflation and interest rates than energy shocks of yore.

By the numbers: Oil futures for delivery in 2027 — contracts to buy or sell crude next year — have climbed to their highest levels since the Iran war began.

  • Prices for January 2027 are up 17% since early September, to more than $97 a barrel.
  • Markets still anticipate some relief next year, but considerably less than they expected just weeks ago. It's a reversal from late summer, when hopes of easing tensions with Iran and a recovery in Middle Eastern oil supplies briefly pushed futures lower.
  • June futures have jumped 18%, to $88 a barrel, while December futures are up 13%, to about $81.

State of play: Crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf, including shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes, surpassed prewar levels in the week ending Oct. 18, according to the Wall Street Journal. But the costly workarounds enabling that recovery have their limits.

  • Those include ship-to-ship transfers outside the Strait of Hormuz, where security risks have deterred some vessels.
  • "You're coming up against limitations on actually how much volume you can move out of the Middle East, even with these processes," Christopher Haines, global head of oil at Energy Aspects, tells Axios.
  • Restoring confidence among shipping companies and insurers that vessels won't be attacked will be "exceptionally hard," Haines adds.

Zoom in: Economist Robin Brooks argues that oil prices reflect higher shipping costs and fears of further attacks more than actual shortages.

  • Using earlier monthly data, he estimates that Persian Gulf crude exports had recovered to 91% of prewar levels, with a "temporary fear factor" adding at least $20 a barrel.

What to watch: The Trump administration is seeking to ease fuel prices ahead of the midterms, most recently by allowing more Russian diesel onto the market.

  • But relief may be minimal: Ukrainian attacks have damaged Russian refineries, while sanctions complicate repairs, limiting additional exports, Haines says.

The bottom line: "The market narrative has shifted from "transitory" to "new normal" right before our eyes," Bob Elliot, chief investment officer at Unlimited Funds, wrote Wednesday morning.

item.title: Putin tells Witkoff he is ready to resume direct peace talks, Russia releases U.S. detainee
item.description:
Russian President Vladimir Putin told White House envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday that he "agrees in principle" resuming trilateral peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. to end the war, according to Russian and U.S. officials.

Why it matters: The White House hopes Putin will show more willingness to compromise after President Trump agreed to lift sanctions on Russian diesel sales and took other steps welcomed by Moscow. For now, it seems the only concession Putin agreed to is to negotiate.

Driving the news: During a three-hour meeting in St. Petersburg, Witkoff presented Putin with an updated proposal to end the war in Ukraine. Trump envoy Jared Kushner joined virtually.

  • Before the meeting, Russia released U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, 74, who had spent more than four years in captivity after being seized by Russian troops in eastern Ukraine in April 2022.
  • Putin announced his release at the top of the meeting with Witkoff. "He is at Pulkovo Airport," Putin told Witkoff in front of the cameras.
  • Witkoff in response thanked Putin and called him "a humanitarian." Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) expressed outrage at Witkoff's comment.
  • "WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of 'humanitarian'. What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say," Tillis wrote on X. Cornyn wrote: "No. Putin is stone cold killer."
  • "Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family. The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return - an unprecedented situation for Russia. There was no 'swap' necessary for this release," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

State of play: Witkoff arrived in Russia after a day of talks in Oslo, Norway, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland and representatives from France, the U.K., Germany, Poland, the EU and NATO.

  • Zelensky said Tuesday that the next step should be a trilateral meeting between him, Putin and Trump — a format Russia has so far rejected.
  • The discussions in Oslo focused on developing a unified proposal for a "framework agreement" to end the war.

What he's saying: "I believe the talks [in Oslo] were productive, and I would like to say that there is progress, and I will update you on this. I hope that we have truly laid the groundwork for a successful end to hostilities in this Ukrainian-Russian conflict," Witkoff told Putin.

  • Witkoff asked Putin to "consider resuming trilateral talks involving Ukraine, Russia, and the United States, where we could discuss the next steps toward achieving a settlement."
  • Witkoff said the talks could include representatives of technical groups of specialists who could discuss these issues in detail.
  • "We have brought several documents outlining approaches to achieving a peaceful settlement in the Ukrainian-Russian conflict. I would ask you, Mr. President, to review these documents a little later," Witkoff said.

The other side: After the meeting, Putin's foreign policy adviser, Yuri Ushakov, told Russian reporters that Putin agreed to hold trilateral talks between negotiation teams.

  • "Our president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, ready to resume the aforementioned trilateral negotiations on the main topic around the 10th of November," he said, adding that the talks could take place in Abu Dhabi.
  • Ushakov claimed Putin was ready to resume the trilateral talks several weeks ago, but the Ukrainian strikes on Russia on the day of the parliamentary elections led to their cancelation.
  • Putin's adviser said Witkoff briefed Putin on the discussions in Oslo. "The Oslo talks didn't contain much that was useful in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis," Ushakov said.

The latest: A U.S. official said Witkoff and Kushner proposed a trilateral meeting at the technical level between the U.S., Russia, and Ukraine. "This was accepted by the Ukrainians in Oslo yesterday and by the Russians in St. Petersburg today," the official said.

The intrigue: Putin also told Witkoff he wants to discuss the possibility of Russia mediating between the U.S. and Iran.

  • "You know that we have a special, trusting relationship with Iran, with our partners in Iran, our friends, built over decades, and if there's anything we can do to resolve this crisis, we'll be happy to do so. You're also well aware of our proposals in this area," Putin said.

What's next: Putin told Witkoff he wants to discuss a possible meeting with Trump in China in mid-November.
