item.title: "I am giving you money!" Nvidia's CEO wants every country to build its own AI
item.description:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is crisscrossing Europe with a multibillion-dollar checkbook and a grand ambition: Make his company the indispensable backbone of the global AI economy.

Why it matters: As fears of an AI bubble rattle Wall Street, Huang is working to spread the boom beyond the U.S. and China — courting governments, bankrolling startups and cultivating massive new markets for Nvidia's chips.

The big picture: The godfather of AI is trying to single-handedly build a new market for Nvidia chips, betting that governments and institutions around the world will want their own, highly customized data centers running open models.

  • If it works, it could shore up demand for Nvidia chips just as another big group of customers — neoclouds — appear financially shaky.

Driving the news: Part showman, part salesman, Huang has spent the past week preaching the gospel of AI across Europe ahead of a keynote Wednesday at Nvidia's flagship conference in Berlin.

  • In France, Huang announced investments in four startups and joked, whisky glass in hand, that he's "the biggest VC in Europe." President Emmanuel Macron welcomed him to Paris, while France's economy minister compared the AI revolution to the Gold Rush.
  • In Britain, Huang channeled Oprah Winfrey while announcing stakes in five startups. "I am giving you money! And I am giving you money! And I am giving you money!" he shouted from the stage of a converted London church.
  • In Sweden, Huang unveiled a supercomputer backed by the country's industrial elite, likening Nvidia's technology to a "time machine" capable of compressing years of scientific research into days.
  • In Germany, Huang challenged Chancellor Friedrich Merz to loosen Europe's regulatory instincts. "There's nothing to regulate if the industry doesn't thrive," he warned Monday. "Give Germany a chance. Give this industry a chance."

Zoom in: At the heart of Huang's global strategy is "sovereign AI" — the idea that every nation should build and control its own AI infrastructure, data and models, rather than depend on U.S. or Chinese tech giants.

  • In addition to roughly $10 billion in investments in Europe, Nvidia is helping build national AI ecosystems across Saudi Arabia, South Korea, India, Malaysia and Africa.
  • For Huang, the prize is a vast new class of customers, including entire countries that see AI infrastructure as an economic and national security imperative.

Between the lines: Huang's global offensive comes at a precarious moment for the AI industry, with Wall Street increasingly questioning whether the technology's enormous promise can justify its astronomical costs.

  • Shares and bonds of Nvidia-backed CoreWeave and other "neocloud" providers have plunged, fueling fears that the companies borrowing billions to buy Nvidia's chips may struggle to pay their debts.
  • Investors are also scrutinizing a circular flow of money in which Nvidia helps finance the very companies buying its products, raising questions about how much demand is self-sustaining.

What to watch: Huang has emerged as the AI industry's chief cheerleader during periods of market turmoil, countering predictions of a bubble with assurances that demand is still accelerating.

  • His Berlin keynote offered another chance to calm investors by arguing that the next wave of AI spending will come from governments treating the technology as a national necessity, not a speculative bet.
  • Nvidia announced a number of initiatives oriented around the "AI factories" theme at the Berlin event, including a design for modular computing pods that can be quickly deployeds, and a "full-stack" option to offer "sovereign" AI solutions by combining the company's chips and a new family of open-weight models.

The bottom line: Countries racing to secure their independence in the AI age may find themselves more reliant than ever on one American company.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details from the event.

item.title: The permitting bill enters a critical stretch
item.description:
Data: Columbia University Center on Global Energy Policy; Table: Ben Geman/Axios

The push to pass a sweeping permitting bill is gaining powerful allies and encountering fresh resistance as Congress prepares for a post-midterms showdown.

Why it matters: It's the most important energy bill in a long time.

  • Cutting hurdles for projects is a top priority for fossil fuels and renewables sectors.
  • But some environmentalists say it badly weakens crucial protections in the name of speeding reviews.

Driving the news: A new, interactive analysis out on Wednesday projects potentially huge time savings if the bill becomes law.

  • Transmission projects could see the biggest acceleration, per Jack Andreasen Cavanaugh, a researcher with Columbia's energy think tank.
  • He based it on historical data about a large number of specific projects, then estimated how much quicker they would have proceeded under the bill.
  • Columbia's Center on Global Energy Policy doesn't have an institutional position on the bill. But founding director Jason Bordoff, a prominent voice in energy policy circles, is urging environmentalists not to oppose it.

State of play: A who's who of economic and national security officials spanning six presidents (including Trump) are linking arms behind the bill in a new letter to Capitol Hill leaders.

What's next: The effort goes beyond signatures for some of the former officials, according to letter organizer Arnab Datta of the Institute for Progress, a nonpartisan think tank.

  • "Some folks are engaging beyond the letter itself with stakeholders across the board, and some have made themselves available for members briefings or conversations," he tells me via email.

Catch up quick: The letter from 19 officials includes Biden-era Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen and Trump 1.0 Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, among five people who held the job.

  • The list also features Trump 1.0 Secretary of State and CIA boss Mike Pompeo, and Leon Panetta, who had top Obama-era defense and CIA gigs, to name just two others.

Friction point: The last 24 hours has also brought new signs of simmering opposition to the bill, or at least parts of it, adding to existing concerns among tribal leaders and some green groups.

  • Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) posted on X that it would be "tone deaf if Congress makes it easier to build data centers."
  • That drew pushback from backers who emphasized provisions to ensure data center companies cover grid costs.

What we're watching: The Edison Electric Institute, a powerful group of for-profit utilities, still hasn't weighed in.

  • But David Pomerantz, who's with the progressive Energy & Policy Institute obtained an Oklahoma Gas & Electric document criticizing the transmission provisions.

The bottom line: The Senate is expected to hold a procedural vote on the bipartisan permitting bill immediately after lawmakers return from recess.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

Catch up quick: The letter from 19 officials includes Biden-era Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen and Trump 1.0 Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, among five people who held the job.

  • The list also features Trump 1.0 Secretary of State and CIA boss Mike Pompeo, and Leon Panetta, who had top Obama-era defense and CIA gigs, to name just two others.

Friction point: The last 24 hours has also brought new signs of simmering opposition to the bill, or at least parts of it, adding to existing concerns among tribal leaders and some green groups.

  • Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) posted on X that it would be "tone deaf if Congress makes it easier to build data centers."
  • That drew pushback from backers who emphasized provisions to ensure data center companies cover grid costs.

What we're watching: The Edison Electric Institute, a powerful group of for-profit utilities, still hasn't weighed in.

  • But David Pomerantz, who's with the progressive Energy & Policy Institute obtained an Oklahoma Gas & Electric document criticizing the transmission provisions.

The bottom line: The Senate is expected to hold a procedural vote on the bipartisan permitting bill immediately after lawmakers return from recess.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: AI is getting better at hacking power and water systems, new research shows
item.description:
The world's most advanced AI models are suddenly capable of blueprinting cyberattacks on critical services like power grids and water systems with alarming success rates, according to new research.

Why it matters: Critical infrastructure operators are running out of time. Top-tier frontier models are dangerously adept at mapping out attacks, new research from cybersecurity company Frenos shows, and it's only a matter of time before freely available AI models make such hacks easier to execute.

  • "It's a clock that is moving faster than we've ever seen," Steve Swick, former top security executive at American Electric Power, told reporters during a briefing.

Driving the news: Researchers at Frenos tested 10 AI models on their ability to plan attacks against industrial systems, such as the software that monitors water treatment processes.

  • Three out of 10 models tested successfully constructed attack plans in roughly 90% of attempts.
  • Performance varied widely: Three models the researchers considered to be at the frontier of capabilities succeeded in just 17.9% to 31.9% of attempts.
  • The strongest foreign open-weight model succeeded 36.2% of the time, while the strongest U.S. open-weight model succeeded just 5.2%.
  • Frenos did not disclose the names of the models tested.

Zoom in: The research included nearly 17,000 tests, including 2,520 attempts to construct complete attack plans.

  • The models received information about potential targets and were tasked with piecing together the steps needed to achieve specific objectives.

The big picture: Critical services like water systems and manufacturing plants have long been targets for nation-state adversaries and cybercriminals.

  • Many operators face staffing and budget constraints. Testing and upgrading their systems can also risk disruptions to essential services that they can't afford.
  • Unlike traditional corporate networks, industrial systems can be sensitive to unexpected traffic and commands. Even an unsuccessful attack attempt could disrupt essential operations.

Threat level: Once attackers gain access to an industrial network, AI could help them quietly map out systems and identify weaknesses without the same time constraints facing human hackers, Frenos co-founder and CTO Harry Thomas said.

  • "AI doesn't have the problem with patience," Thomas said. "It doesn't need to eat. It doesn't need to sleep, and it doesn't need to use the restroom."
  • Paul Shaver, head of operational technology at cybersecurity firm Armadin, added that AI agents can already conduct reconnaissance and analyze large volumes of data without necessarily triggering security alerts.

The intrigue: Thomas said the researchers used a relatively simple setup to guide the models through their tasks. More sophisticated tools that provide additional context and feedback could improve their performance.

  • "A more capable harness could have given these AI models more of an edge," he said.

What to watch: Several initiatives — including from the White House, frontier AI companies, and cybersecurity organizations — have cropped up in recent weeks to help lower the costs and provide resources for critical infrastructure organizations.

Go deeper: Frightening AI advances speed race to secure critical infrastructure

item.title: OpenAI brings its frontier models to rival Google Cloud
item.description:
OpenAI is bringing its AI models and Codex coding tools to Google Cloud, expanding its reach to customers of all three major U.S. cloud providers — including companies that are also among its fiercest AI rivals.

Why it matters: The move underscores a growing recognition that winning the enterprise AI race isn't just about building the smartest models. It's also about making those models available wherever businesses already run their software and store their data.

  • For OpenAI, the agreement offers another way to reach corporate customers without requiring them to establish a separate relationship with the ChatGPT maker.
  • For Google, it means selling a competitor's AI models alongside its own Gemini offerings, potentially capturing business that might otherwise go to rival cloud providers.

Driving the news: Under the agreement announced Wednesday, Google Cloud customers will be able to purchase OpenAI's frontier models through Google's "Model Garden and Marketplace," including by using existing cloud spending commitments.

  • The deal also brings OpenAI models to Google's Antigravity development environment and Gemini Agent.
  • General availability is planned in the coming weeks.

The big picture: The agreement follows OpenAI's expansion onto Amazon Web Services earlier this year, after changes to its Microsoft partnership opened the door to broader cloud distribution.

  • AWS CEO Matt Garman said at the time that customers had long wanted to run OpenAI models where their existing applications and data already resided.
  • Amazon has since expanded the OpenAI models and services available through its Bedrock platform, although neither company has publicly quantified the additional business generated by the arrangement.

What they're saying: Mike Leone, VP and analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, said the deal is significant for both companies, particularly because many Google Cloud customers want access to OpenAI models without moving their data.

  • "For Google, I read the deal as confidence, because Gemini now has to win those customers with OpenAI sitting right next to it," Leone told Axios.
  • But he doesn't see Google as necessarily hurting Gemini, since customers will still pay Google for its cloud platform, data services and security regardless of which AI models they choose.

Yes, but: Distribution is only part of the equation. OpenAI still has to persuade enterprises to choose its models over those from Google, Anthropic and other competitors, many of which are available through the same cloud platforms.

  • That could make the cloud providers' existing enterprise relationships and infrastructure as important as the models they offer.
  • "Once every cloud has the top models, I think the competitive advantage goes to whoever does the best job with a company's data, governance, and costs," Leone said.

item.title: Executives are more likely to trust AI over themselves
item.description:
Executives are twice as likely as rank-and-file workers to trust AI over their own judgment, per a survey out Wednesday morning.

Why it matters: It's a worrying development. Leaders are hired for their experience and knowledge.

  • Outsourcing that to AI raises the risk of making decisions that don't line up with reality, which then reverberate across companies and beyond.

By the numbers: 32.8% of executives said that they trust AI more than their own judgment, according to the survey from Charter, a workplace research and media company.

  • That's twice the rate for workers, or individual contributors. Just 16.3% of individual contributors said the same.
  • The divide shows up at the level below executives — 34.8% of managers said they trust AI more than their own judgment.

Zoom out: "Cognitive offloading" is a term for using tools like AI to reduce mental effort.

  • "Executives—despite having the most experience—are doing it more than anyone," the report's co-authors wrote.

The fine print: Charter in August surveyed 5,002 U.S. office workers, at companies with at least 100 employees, who said they use AI at work, including 2,952 individual contributors, 1,547 managers and 503 executives — including vice presidents, C-suite executives, owners and founders.

Between the lines: Most executives are under a lot of pressure to know the answers to a lot of questions really quickly — and AI can help with that at least in the short term, says report co-author Brian Elliott, a former Slack executive who is now executive-in-residence at Charter and co-wrote the report.

  • AI "lends itself very well to the 'seldom wrong, never in doubt' tendency that some executives have," he says.
  • "If you feel like you have to fake it until you make it as an executive, then AI is certainly going to feed those tendencies because you can appear to be really smart, really quick."

Zoom in: He described tech executives who use AI to build product prototypes over a weekend, then expect their teams to quickly turn those into functioning products — without appreciating the more complicated work involved.

  • "AI is really good at giving you the executive summary. It's not necessarily as good at giving you the very specific answer to the problem you've got today, which is more often what an individual contributor faces."

Reality check: The Charter survey measures executives' self-reported trust in AI, but not whether they actually follow its advice when making consequential decisions.

  • The report's findings were overall positive about AI's potential in the workplace. 42.7% of AI users said it improved both their work and personal lives.

Friction point: A key tension for workers is the threat of AI job loss, the researchers observed in separate qualitative interviews with 91 more workers.

  • The better workers become with AI, the more they realize how much can be done without them, the survey found.
  • There's a "persistent tension."

The bottom line: Executives are mostly free from that tension, says Elliott.

  • "The odds that an AI CEO shows up and takes over a company are excruciatingly low."

item.title: Inside the "To Catch a Predator" election's ad wars
item.description:
Republicans and Democrats are flooding the midterm airwaves with explosive TV ads accusing their opponents of protecting pedophiles and child sexual abusers.

Why it matters: The advertising blitz underscores the lingering power of the Jeffrey Epstein scandal, which has fueled distrust of powerful figures and pushed allegations of child sexual abuse to the forefront of national politics.

  • The controversy over the Trump administration's handling of the Epstein files — including allegations that officials sought to protect powerful figures by not releasing all of the files — has kept the issue in the headlines.
  • The midterm ads that have followed have been bipartisan and are playing out in state and federal races.

By the numbers: Since Sept. 1, candidates and outside groups have aired at least $70 million in TV ads mentioning pedophilia, Epstein and allegations related to child sexual abuse, according to AdImpact.

  • Of the 118 ads identified, 63 were sponsored by Democrats, 52 by Republicans and three by independents.

Driving the news: The issue has become a flashpoint in the competitive Senate race in Kansas, where Democrats unveiled three ads Tuesday attacking Republican Sen. Roger Marshall over his initial vote against a measure to force the Justice Department to release additional Epstein files.

  • Meanwhile, the conservative Club for Growth has been airing an ad accusing pastor Adam Hamilton, Marshall's Democratic opponent, of mishandling sexual abuse allegations involving a church camp volunteer.
  • The allegations date to 2005, when church leaders initially investigated accusations involving boys at the camp rather than immediately contacting police. Hamilton has released a commercial in which he denies a cover-up.
  • The Club for Growth's ad closely resembles promotional materials for the new movie "Primetime," which is inspired by the former NBC TV series "To Catch a Predator."

In Texas, Democrats backing Senate candidate James Talarico have spent more than $8 million on ads attacking his opponent, state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), over his office's initial offer of a plea deal calling for just one day in jail for a man accused of sexually abusing a child.

  • Paxton says he agreed to the deal to spare a child abuse victim from having to testify in court a second time.

In North Carolina, meanwhile, Democrats have aired four ads accusing Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley of appointing a convicted sex offender to a state GOP committee. Whatley has denied hiring the man.

  • "It's an issue that goes to character and judgment," said John Anzalone, a veteran Democratic pollster who's advising Whatley's Democratic opponent, former Gov. Roy Cooper.

Behind the scenes: Private GOP polling in Kansas, provided to Axios, illustrates why strategists believe the attacks can resonate.

  • After hearing allegations about Hamilton's handling of the church camp incident, 69% of Kansas voters surveyed said they were less likely to support him, strategists found.

State of play: Republicans' embrace of the attacks marks a striking turn for a party that spent months on the defensive over the Trump administration's resistance to releasing additional Epstein files.

  • Some GOP strategists see the attacks as a way to put Democrats on defense as Republicans struggle to sell voters on Trump's agenda.
  • Democrats have spent much of the campaign hammering Republicans over high prices. But with voters' views on the economy largely set, attack ads are increasingly focused on issues of character and judgment.

What they're saying: "Epstein reinforced the suspicion that powerful people protect each other and operate under different rules," Republican pollster Chris Wilson told Axios.

  • "Allegations involving children are especially visceral, and [the collapse of trust in institutions] gives them added resonance."

item.title: Why Anthropic can't afford to delay its IPO
item.description:
Anthropic's impending IPO will test a jittery Wall Street, but investors say the timing isn't optional. The reason is simple math: The AI giant has grown too big for private fundraising.

Why it matters: Top AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI are racking up 12-figure spending commitments, straining the financial system's ability to keep up with a buildout that rivals America's railroads or interstate highways.

  • With private borrowing costs spiking, tapping the massive liquidity of the public markets is the best way to fund the next phase of the AI arms race, investors say.

State of play: Anthropic's computing commitments could reach $750 billion in the coming years, according to a draft IPO prospectus seen by the Wall Street Journal.

  • The company already faces more than $600 billion in future infrastructure costs and is negotiating additional deals that could add another $150 billion.
  • While Anthropic generated $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, up from $1.1 billion a year earlier, the company also disclosed an $80.7 billion net loss over the same period, though most of that is tied to accounting charges related to fundraising, per WSJ.

Zoom in: That math points to a numbers problem that can only be solved by public markets, investors tell Axios.

  • OpenAI's most recent fundraising round — the biggest in history — is a case in point. It took the company months to secure more than $120 billion in financing, a historic feat that is unlikely to be repeated in this market climate.
  • While demand for Anthropic shares is absurdly high — just ask the guy who offered up his near-$5 million home to get some — the souring market climate significantly raises the stakes for a public listing. If it goes well, it could help reset investor angst about the stability of the AI boom.
  • Public markets will provide a deeper pool of financing as Anthropic expands beyond traditional venture capital.

Follow the money: The pool of cash on the private markets side is getting harder to tap.

  • Anthropic is offering Blackstone a yield exceeding 10% on $9 billion in junior debt as part of a record $60 billion chip-financing package, according to the Financial Times.
  • That's above the 8.5% rate on an earlier financing deal, suggesting private investors are demanding greater compensation for taking on AI-related risks.

Between the lines: Private markets have done the heavy lifting on AI investing long enough, and they're ready for somebody else to carry the load.

  • Anthropic was widely expected to go public in September before one of its researchers quit and a raft of safety incidents brought new public awareness to AI safety concerns.
  • Now, Anthropic is expected to IPO before Thanksgiving.

Zoom out: The IPO follows anxiety on Wall Street regarding the AI trade, especially as companies specializing in renting computing capacity and building data centers confront market skepticism.

  • Nvidia-backed Australian data center company Firmus scrapped its planned IPO amid market volatility.
  • South Korean AI cloud provider Elice saw its shares plunge 32% in their trading debut despite rapid revenue growth.
  • Meanwhile, concerns about AI infrastructure debt have pushed borrowing costs for CoreWeave sharply higher, with yields on some of its bonds approaching 15%.

Reality check: Anthropic isn't just any AI startup.

  • One Anthropic investor told Axios the company is simply ready to go public given its size and maturity.
  • The investor also described Anthropic's latest financial results as "spectacular," pushing back on concerns about slowing revenue growth.

The bottom line: Anthropic may have to go public in less than perfect conditions, but investors see an IPO as the best way to put the AI boom to the market's ultimate test.

item.title: When AI models refuse to fight hackers
item.description:
In the race to fend off AI-enabled cyber threats, security teams are confronting a new problem: The AI models they rely on to investigate attacks can suddenly refuse to help.

Why it matters: While AI giants race to build AI tools that can respond quickly to hacking or other malicious online threats, strict guardrails on their most powerful models lock out defenders mid-investigation, leaving them scrambling for alternatives at critical moments.

What's happening: OpenCode, an open-source AI coding agent, said it was compromised over the weekend, allowing attackers to obtain API keys belonging to some customers, including keys for OpenAI, Anthropic and Google services.

  • OpenCode said the breach was "related to a large scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users."
  • OpenCode co-creator Dax Raad said attackers had been targeting its systems continuously for 48 hours, forcing the company to keep its own AI agents running around the clock to respond.
  • OpenAI, Google and Anthropic have said they worked with affected customers to revoke exposed API keys and address unauthorized usage charges.

Zoom in: Raad said on X that frontier AI models initially helped investigate the breach but then "started refusing."

  • The models' safety restrictions reportedly began blocking requests as the investigation turned to potentially malicious code, even though OpenCode was trying to defend its own systems.
  • OpenCode then gained access to OpenAI's Daybreak Blue program, which gives vetted cybersecurity defenders access to models with fewer restrictions.
  • "We definitely need to be more proactive and we've made so many improvements over the last few days," Raad wrote on X Monday.

The big picture: The incident underscored a dilemma facing cybersecurity teams trying to figure out when to use powerful proprietary AI models, which come with built-in restrictions, or open-weight alternatives that offer greater control over how they're deployed.

  • When Hugging Face discovered suspicious activity on its systems that it later linked to OpenAI's own agents, its security team turned to a Chinese open-weight model to help investigate after encountering restrictions on frontier models.

Yes, but: AI companies maintain that they need to gate access to their most powerful models to ensure that malicious actors can't abuse their cyber capabilities.

Between the lines: Cybersecurity teams will have to figure out how to balance the need for faster AI-powered defenses with restrictions designed to keep those same capabilities out of attackers' hands, Chris Jones, chief technology officer at Nightwing, told Axios.

  • "We're all going to have to figure out how that race gets modulated over time," Jones said. "That's a big piece here."

Go deeper: Anthropic and OpenAI are now cybersecurity's kingmakers

item.title: Exclusive: Ramaswamy doubles down on explosive ad featuring rival's mother, despite backlash
item.description:
Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign for Ohio governor is pouring $4 million into a bombshell ad in which his opponent's estranged mother attacks her daughter — doubling down on the message despite fierce bipartisan backlash, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: Ramaswamy is gambling that the deeply personal attack by Amy Acton's mother — who Acton has said sided with her stepfather after he sexually assaulted Acton when she was 12 — will resonate with voters.

  • After the ad began appearing Tuesday on social media, many fellow Republicans urged Ramaswamy to distance his campaign from it.
  • They warned it could backfire at a time when the controversy over the Epstein files has elevated the sexual abuse of children as a national campaign issue.

Driving the news: Ramaswamy's campaign confirmed to Axios that it produced the ad, which began circulating on social media late Monday without language identifying its sponsor.

  • Sources close to Ramaswamy's campaign said the ad tested well with "persuadable" voters, prompting the decision to launch a $4 million statewide campaign that began streaming Tuesday night.

Catch up quick: The minute-long commercial features Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, accusing her daughter of lying about her childhood and urging Ohioans not to vote for her.

  • "She lies about her past," Arthur says. "She's lied her entire life."
  • Arthur also disputes Acton's account of experiencing homelessness as a child.

The other side: Acton, a physician, has said she was sexually abused at age 12 by her stepfather, who faced criminal charges, and that her mother sided with him.

  • Acton and her brother were removed from their mother's custody. According to her brother, their mother remained married to Acton's alleged abuser until his death.
  • Acton, 60, has said she hasn't seen her mother since childhood.

In a statement posted to Facebook on Tuesday, Acton said that "between the ages of 10 and 12, I was sexually abused by her husband, while my birth mother did nothing to protect me."

  • "I've always known that she was deeply sick and unwell, and it's sad to see Vivek Ramaswamy exploit her all for his own political gain."
  • Acton's brother, Philip Stearns, called Ramaswamy's ad "disgusting."

What they're saying: Despite bipartisan criticism, Ramaswamy's campaign continued to treat the mother's statements as campaign gold.

  • "This is a campaign-ending moment for Amy Acton. The people who know her best keep warning Ohioans about her," Ramaswamy campaign manager Jonathan Ewing told Axios.

Several prominent Republicans and conservative commentators blasted the ad, arguing that it could generate sympathy for Acton.

  • Republican strategist David Urban on CNN drew a parallel to the Epstein controversy, warning that voters are especially sympathetic to victims of sexual assault and that the ad could backfire.
  • "It seems crazy to me one would assume this would work and not backfire," conservative commentator Mary Katharine Ham posted on X.

Yes, but: Some conservatives defended the commercial, including Donald Trump Jr., who urged Ohio voters to "watch [it] and think about what it means."

By the numbers: A mid-October Marist survey showed Acton leading Ramaswamy 50% to 43% among likely voters.

What's next: Ramaswamy and Republican Sen. Jon Husted are set to campaign with Vice President Vance in Cincinnati on Wednesday.

item.title: House Democrats forced to make tough choices with limited midterm cash
item.description:
House Democrats' main super PAC is winding down its spending in several races where the party has struggled to make headway despite national trends working in their favor.

Why it matters: Democrats' ambitions of winning heavily Republican districts are running into the reality of finite resources at the end of a long and expensive midterm campaign.

  • The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and its corresponding super PAC, House Majority PAC, have struggled to keep pace with their GOP counterparts' monster fundraising this cycle.
  • Republicans also have the bonus advantage of a network of cash-rich outside groups, namely President Trump's MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk's America PAC.

Driving the news: HMP pulled back its spending this week in three Republican-leaning districts, according to AdImpact and a source familiar with the matter.

TN-05: Democrats were bullish about their star recruit, Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder, until redistricting made the district redder and embattled Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) lost his primary to former state Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher.

  • HMP has drawn down its ad reservations in the district from nearly $1.6 million this month to a little over $500,000 as of Monday.
  • Trump carried the newly reconstituted 5th district by 21 percentage points in 2024. Cook Political Report rates the race as "solidly Republican."

FL-07: Facing a situation similar to Tennessee, Democrats liked their odds of unseating scandal-tarred Rep. Cory Mills (R-Fla.), who lost his primary to former local news anchor Ryan Elijah.

  • Like Molder, Democratic candidate Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff, was a top DCCC recruit and is part of the committee's coveted "Red to Blue" program.
  • HMP essentially halved its investment in the district on Monday, cutting ad reservations from $3.9 million to just $1.95 million.
  • Cook rates the race as "likely Republican," though a poll released by the DCCC on Tuesday had the two candidates tied at 45% each.

CO-03: A top target for Democrats when Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) represented it, the seat has become a heavier lift for the party since she abandoned it and Rep. Jeff Hurd (R-Colo.) took office last year.

  • Democrat Dwayne Romero, a real estate company CEO and Army veteran, is seen by party operatives as having failed to build the kind of momentum shown by Jessica Killin in the neighboring 5th District.
  • HMP halved its investment in this district too, from more than $2.1 million last week to less than $1.1 million as of Monday.

Between the lines: The group has also made partial cuts — what it calls "shaves" — in districts where Democrats have struggled to gain traction but still see a glimmer of hope.

  • That includes Arizona's 2nd District, where Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.) is locked in a rematch with former Navajo Nation President Jonathan Nez in a race Cook rates as "likely Republican."
  • HMP has also taken some money out of Texas' 23rd District, where Republican Brandon Herrera, a right-wing YouTuber, is facing Democratic lawyer Katy Padilla Stout in another race rated "likely Republican."

Yes, but: Some HMP triages are in districts where they feel confident the Democratic candidate will prevail.

  • That includes Reps. Greg Landsman (D-Ohio) and Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Mich.), both of whose races are rated "likely Democratic" by Cook.
  • The PAC has also pulled back in the districts of retiring Reps. Darrell Issa (R-Calif.) and Don Bacon (R-Neb.), which Democrats are increasingly bullish about flipping.

The money from these cuts is funneled to districts the party views as more core battlegrounds — including some seats Trump carried by double digits in 2024 that Democrats nevertheless view as winnable.

  • HMP has added at least $4.7 million to its existing investments in nearly two dozen districts over the last two days.

What they're saying: Phil Gardner, a senior adviser for Blue Dog Action — a centrist group backing Dalton — told Axios of the cuts in Florida, "I'm not sure what HMP was thinking here."

  • "The rest of the party is not triaging this seat," he said, citing the DCCC's poll and House Minority Whip Katherine Clark's (D-Mass.) plans to campaign there on Wednesday.
  • Gardner said he agrees with "95% of the decisions HMP's made this cycle," but that it is "bonkers they're dumping so much money" into Maine's 2nd District "while leaving one of the party's best recruits high and dry in Florida."
  • Blue Dog Action spent nearly $500,000 to help Dalton win the primary, but it hasn't yet invested any money in the general election.

The bottom line: "We're focused on taking back the House," CJ Warnke, a spokesperson for HMP, told Axios in response to Gardner's criticism.

  • Said Gardner: "I'm confident they'll rethink and make the right decision for the final week. Bale can win and hold that seat with everyone's help."

item.title: Witkoff to present Putin with peace proposal after talks with Zelensky
item.description:
White House envoy Steve Witkoff will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday and present him with an updated proposal to end the war in Ukraine, a U.S. official said.

  • President Trump's son-in-law and adviser Jared Kushner will join the meeting virtually.

Why it matters: The White House hopes Putin will show more willingness to compromise after Trump agreed to lift sanctions on Russian diesel sales and took other steps welcomed by Moscow.

Driving the news: Witkoff will arrive in Russia after a day of talks in Oslo, Norway, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland and representatives from France, the UK, Germany, Poland, the EU and NATO.

  • Zelensky said Tuesday that the next step should be a trilateral meeting between him, Putin and Trump — a format Russia has so far rejected.
  • The U.S. hopes the new proposal will "create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations," a U.S. official said.

Zoom in: The discussions in Oslo focused on developing a unified proposal for a "framework agreement" to end the war.

  • The U.S. official said Ukraine "brought forward new ideas and proposals, which were discussed in detail."
  • The official said the parties made "meaningful progress" and now have "strong alignment at the working level" on next steps.

Behind the scenes: Kushner joined the meeting virtually and again pressed Trump's demand that Ukraine halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, according to a source with knowledge.

  • "Jared was very direct," the person said.
  • Zelensky said after the meeting that he's prepared to cease strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow takes reciprocal steps.

What he's saying: Trump said Tuesday that he thinks "Russia would like to get it done," but he expressed doubt that Zelensky wants to end the war.

  • "If he does not, it's gonna be a very bad thing," Trump added. "We want Zelensky to make a deal … If they don't make a deal, it's just gonna get worse [for Ukraine]."

item.title: Exclusive: House GOP clings to 2026 fundraising lead
item.description:
House Republicans are entering the final two weeks of the midterms with a rare but razor-thin fundraising advantage over House Democrats.

Why it matters: Democrats outraised Republicans by $84 million in 2024 and $74 million in 2022. Now, Republicans are holding their own financially even as they face mounting political headwinds.

  • The National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) outraised the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) by $1 million ($250 million to $249 million) so far this cycle, Axios has learned.
  • "The NRCC spent this cycle building a war chest to amplify Republican wins and make Democrats answer for their failures," NRCC Chair Richard Hudson (R-N.C.) told Axios in a statement.

By the numbers: The NRCC raised $50 million in the third quarter of 2026 and entered October with $61 million cash on hand.

  • The DCCC raised $50.5 million in Q3, and entered October with $55.7 million cash on hand.
  • The NRCC raised $28.5 million in September (the last month of Q3) including a $14 million transfer from the Republican National Committee, compared to $26.3 million raised by the DCCC.

Between the lines: Hudson's fundraising success comes as Speaker Mike Johnson has also built a formidable fundraising operation of his own.

  • Johnson has raised more than $220 million for House Republicans since becoming speaker in October 2023, a turnaround from early concerns about whether he could fill the void left by former Speaker Kevin McCarthy.

item.title: Space X and Tesla exploring merger, CEO Elon Musk says
item.description:
SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a potential merger — and Elon Musk thinks "it's a good idea," the CEO of both companies said Tuesday.

Why it matters: SpaceX and Tesla have increasingly been collaborating on chips and AI projects — and Musk leads both companies — prompting widespread speculation that they could join forces.

Driving the news: Musk said on SpaceX's earnings call that the two companies have formed committees of independent directors to explore the possibility of a deal.

  • "Because I'm a conflicted party, I can't actually be in the discussions," he said, but he added that "I think it would be a good idea."

Zoom in: Musk said "there's a lot to be gained" from cooperation on technologies like AI, chips, robotics and connectivity.

  • But he said a deal is not certain.
  • "I think that would be overstating it," he said, noting that 50% of Tesla shareholders would need to approve the deal, which he called a high hurdle.

What they're saying: Tech analyst Gene Munster of Deepwater Asset Management said he believes there's a 95% chance a deal will take place in the next two years.

  • "Believe me, shareholders would support this," Munster said Tuesday on X after Musk made his comments.

Of note: Any combination would be massive: SpaceX has a market cap of more than $2 trillion, while Tesla's is nearly $1.5 trillion.

  • Tesla reports its quarterly results on Wednesday.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

item.title: Trump goes full apocalypse in anti-Dems midterms message
item.description:
President Trump is escalating his doomsday warnings about a Democratic takeover of Congress, painting a nightmarish vision of an America consumed by burning cities, economic collapse, mutilated children and the destruction of Western civilization.

Why it matters: Trump has long portrayed Democrats as an existential threat to the country. But in an effort to preserve Republicans' grip on Washington, he's taking that rhetoric to new extremes as he casts the election as a choice between Republican rule and national catastrophe.

At the same time, Trump is offering voters a financial incentive to keep Republicans in power: $5,000 checks for every adult American citizen if the GOP retains control of Congress.

  • The pledge would cost more than $1 trillion and has no clear path to becoming reality.

What they're saying: "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress," White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Axios in a statement.

  • "The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump's winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats' extreme liberal policies and obstruction."

Reality check: Even if Democrats take control of Congress, Trump will remain president and retain veto power over legislation they pass.

Here's what he's been telling voters.

America will burn like France

On Monday night, Trump told Kansas voters that under Democrats, America will burn like France, which is facing widespread student and union protests over public spending cuts and deficit concerns, per Reuters.

  • "When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to do to America."
  • Trump has blamed the riots in France on immigration, suggesting that border policies under Democratic Party leadership would unleash the same chaos in America.

Yes, but: The unrest in France has been driven by disputes over living costs and public funding. There's no evidence that Democrats in the U.S. want to take up similar forms of violence.

America will fall into another Great Depression

Trump predicts Democrats will cause economic catastrophe and trigger a depression similar to the one that began in 1929.

  • "If the Democrats win you will have a 1929-style economic depression," Trump told Tennessee voters on Saturday. "I hope I'm wrong on that."

By the numbers: Unemployment peaked at roughly 25% during the Great Depression, compared with about 4% today.

What's next: House Democrats, should they gain power, plan to repeal Trump's tariff policy, bring back Affordable Care Act tax breaks and undo Medicaid cuts as part of a general affordability push.

Democrats will "mutilate your children"

In Arizona, Trump warned last week that Democrats want to "mutilate, cut your children."

  • "I mean, they can do whatever they want, and they do. Your son leaves as Jimmy and comes back home in three days as Janet, and they don't even ask you," Trump said.
  • "They can take your child out of school and do whatever the hell they want."

Reality check: Trump's claims about schools secretly performing gender-transition procedures misrepresent how such medical care works.

  • Schools cannot perform gender-transition surgeries. Those operations take place in medical settings under relevant state laws.

Democrats will "get rid of the border"

Trump warned Democrats would dismantle the border and allow criminals from around the world to enter the U.S.

  • He told voters in Kansas that "the Dumocrat agenda is a plan to extinguish Western civilization. They want to open the borders."
  • Trump claimed prisons around the world will empty prisoners into the United States.

The other side: A coalition of Democrats have proposed using advanced technology to protect the border, while rejecting mass deportation strategies.

Trump: Democrats will take your guns — and wild animals will feast

Trump also warned that Democrats will "take away your guns" if they control Congress.

  • "You know who would love that to happen? Some of the wild animals you have up here that like eating you," he told voters in Montana. "... They would gain a lot of weight."

Context: Mainstream Democrats have not called for repealing the Second Amendment.

  • While some Democrats support banning certain types of guns, that's different from eliminating the constitutional right to own firearms.

Democrats will destroy farms

Trump also warned that Democrats would "decimate Kansas farms."

  • On Monday, the Trump administration announced $8 billion in relief for farmers facing soaring fuel costs, driven in part by Trump's own policies and the Iran war.

What's going on: Democrats have been making a push in farm country by appealing to rural voters in Kansas and Iowa.

  • House Democrats have also proposed expanding support for rural development and family farms.

item.title: Mystery mailings put Congress and election offices on edge
item.description:
Over three dozen congressional lawmakers and election offices in at least 32 states have been targeted with suspicious letters, many containing a white powder.

Why it matters: The letters have forced evacuations and disrupted election offices just weeks before the 2026 midterms, raising concerns about political intimidation.

Driving the news: Rep. Adam Smith's (D-Wash.) district office received a letter Monday, prompting staff to evacuate.

  • In an emailed statement, Smith's office confirmed it "received a suspicious letter containing a powdery substance, like others sent to Congressional offices across the country."
  • Staff returned to the office Tuesday.

What they're saying: "The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices, and Congressional offices," an FBI spokesperson said in an emailed statement.

  • "Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident."

Catch up quick: The U.S. Capitol Police, the House and Senate sergeants at arms and other officials sent notices to congressional offices last week warning about letters containing suspicious substances and urging staffers to be vigilant.

  • Over 100 letters were estimated to be circulating around the country, law enforcement sources told ABC News.
  • The USCP referred Axios to the FBI for comment.

Here's what we know about the suspicious letters:

Who was targeted

At least three dozen lawmakers have been targeted with the letters, including both Democrats and Republicans.

  • That includes prominent leaders such as Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Sens. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.).

Election offices in at least 32 states were targeted with similarly suspicious letters, according to WIRED.

  • Authorities intercepted many of the letters, including those addressed to election offices in Ohio, Minnesota and Connecticut. But in places like Oklahoma, Arizona and Delaware, the letters arrived and prompted evacuations.

What's inside

Many letters contained a white powder-like substance.

  • So far, preliminary testing of the powder has found no hazardous materials.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) also reported receiving suspicious letters but did not disclose their contents.

  • Nebraska officials received a letter that they didn't open and instead turned over to the FBI for further analysis.

Flashback: The Capitol Police's notice went out on the 25th anniversary of the anthrax attacks that terrified Capitol Hill in the wake of 9/11.

  • On Oct. 15, 2001, a staffer opened an anthrax-laced letter in then-Senate Majority Leader Tom Daschle's office, forcing the Hart Senate Office Building to close for months.
  • Anthrax attacks killed five people that year.

Where are they coming from

Law enforcement has not yet determined where the letters are coming from or if they're part of a coordinated attack.

  • The FBI declined to say if the letters are linked, nor are they confirming "specific instances or letters."
  • However, the bureau told Axios in an emailed statement it is working to identify whoever sent the letters.

Worth noting: Some of the letters claimed to come from the Democratic Socialists of America, the left-wing insurgent organization that denies any involvement.

  • Some letters bore a New York City return address that DSA previously used but has not occupied since 2013, a spokesperson said.
  • DSA did not respond to Axios' request for comment.

Go deeper: AI campaign deepfakes are starting to draw legal threats

item.title: Exclusive: OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio
item.description:
OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio, a startup building AI agents to help pharmaceutical companies manage drug development, the ChatGPT maker shared exclusively with Axios.

Why it matters: Rival AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic are both pushing into science as they look to expand beyond their core competencies in coding and cybersecurity.

State of play: OpenAI will integrate Orchestra's team and technology into Rosalind, its suite of AI models and tools designed for life sciences researchers, the company said.

  • Orchestra's platform allows scientists to delegate tasks like monitoring studies, tracking drug development timelines and identifying potential delays to AI agents.
  • Both companies aim to deploy agents that can connect scientific findings with the decisions and next steps required to advance potential treatments.
  • Financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed.

Between the lines: AI companies don't just want to increase productivity, they want to say they are responsible for, say, curing cancer, solving math, and fundamentally changing every critical industry in the world.

  • Those ambitions have fueled acquisitions from rival AI labs.
  • Anthropic acquired AI biotech startup Coefficient Bio for roughly $400 million in April, according to The Information.

Zoom in: OpenAI introduced its specialized GPT-Rosalind model in April to help researchers tackle complex problems in biology, chemistry and drug discovery.

  • OpenAI has also partnered with pharmaceutical giants including Novo Nordisk and Moderna to bring AI into research and development workflows.
  • OpenAI says developing a new medicine typically takes 10 to 15 years, a timeline it hopes AI can shorten.

Zoom out Anthropic has been making its own aggressive push into life sciences.

  • In June, Anthropic launched Claude Science, an AI-powered research platform that connects scientific databases, analysis tools and specialized agents.
  • In September, the company announced a new biological research lab and said Claude had helped discover a previously unknown enzyme system with similarities to CRISPR, though some scientists said these finders were overblown, per Bloomberg.

The bottom line: The AI race is shifting from building the best models to applying that intelligence across industries.

  • Several AI investors told Axios a key question as AI companies go public is how far they can expand into new markets.

item.title: Homebuilder sentiment is at a 14-year low
item.description:
The AI boom is sucking up all the capital. The Federal Reserve is raising rates to try to cool inflation. And one sector is bearing the brunt of the pain from both: housing.

The big picture: The situation is lose-lose for both homebuilders and homebuyers. Builders are facing more expensive capital and bidding for scarce construction-related resources. Would-be buyers are being quoted some of the highest mortgage rates of this century.

  • New September housing starts data out Tuesday morning puts an exclamation point on what has been a slow-moving disaster for a sector that plays an outsized role in the economic cycle and in Americans' basic living standards.

By the numbers: The number of housing units started by builders fell 5.2% last month, the Census Bureau said, to 1.22 million. It's down 7.4% year over year and near post-pandemic lows.

  • Starts of single-family homes fell 4.6% to their lowest level since March 2023.
  • Pending home sales fell 7.3% last month, the National Association of Realtors said Tuesday morning, to the lowest since the data was tracked going back to 2001.
  • Homebuilder sentiment fell this month to its lowest level since 2012, the National Association of Home Builders said Monday.

State of play: The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was 7.4% earlier this month, Freddie Mac said in its most recent weekly reading. The rate was briefly higher than that in 2023, but has not been consistently above that level since the fall of 2000.

  • That has kept homebuyers on the sidelines — while a parallel rise in borrowing costs for developers has made it harder for new projects to pencil out.
  • In effect, the bottomless demand for capital from AI hyperscalers and the U.S. government has to squeeze something, and that something has been the housing sector.
  • Residential investment has subtracted from overall GDP for five of the last six quarters.

Zoom out: Housing affordability is the crux of Americans' broader dissatisfaction with economic conditions, and all signs point to it getting worse, not better.

  • For all the bipartisan emphasis on increasing housing supply — most prominently in the passage of a law to encourage more building earlier this year — conditions are weighted against a building boom.
  • Housing developers are competing with data center builders for labor and materials like copper, concrete and HVAC equipment.

Of note: Restrictionist immigration policy has also crimped the supply of construction workers.

  • "Nationwide, more than one-third of builders reported immigration enforcement activity in their market areas during the past month, causing construction delays and discouraging legal workers from reporting to work," said NAHB chairman Bill Owens, an Ohio homebuilder, in the sentiment release.

Between the lines: An unfortunate side effect of relying on Fed interest rate policy for macroeconomic stabilization is that interest-sensitive sectors, particularly housing, take it on the chin when the economy shows signs of overheating.

  • It's particularly problematic now, when persistent undersupply of housing is a defining economic challenge of our age.

The bottom line: The current alignment of interest rates, housing supply and construction costs isn't making anybody happy.

  • Builders can't afford to build, buyers can't afford to buy, and even the people sitting pretty with pre-2022 mortgages can't afford to move.

item.title: France riots become Republican midterm boogeyman
item.description:
As the French right-wing National Rally is seizing on fiery protests in the country for its pre-election pitch, so are President Trump and his Republican allies in the U.S.

The big picture: The Trump administration has used the unrest, which began over education grievances, to bolster its messaging on immigration and the threat of "communists," a group Trump has repeatedly claimed is threatening American civilization.

Driving the news: "When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical 'Dumocrats' want to do to America," Trump said before a Kansas rally crowd Monday.

  • He claimed France was being "conquered, looted and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists who hate Christianity" and "the Western civilization itself."
  • Speaking earlier to reporters, the president claimed, without evidence, that the situation in France was about "immigration, not schools." He's repeatedly blamed immigration for the protests.
  • The White House referred Axios to the president's Truth Social post echoing that rhetoric.

Catch up quick: Localized demonstrations by high school students that began in Paris last month have broadened into a massive nationwide movement over poor school conditions and cost of living, sparking thousands of arrests and clashes between police and protesters, Axios' Bec Falconer reports.

  • The civil unrest gave way to rioting and looting, leading French President Emmanuel Macron to condemn "unrestrained violence" by "insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals," per AP.
  • Some 550,000 people demonstrated in France Saturday, per the Interior Ministry, though Reuters reported that a key union estimated 800,000.
  • On the sidelines, "thugs" chose "violence," per a translation of the Interior Ministry's statement, which added that some 500 police officers and firefighters were injured.
  • The forceful police response to student demonstrators has also been scrutinized, sparking dozens of probes into officer conduct.

Zoom out: Some U.S. Republicans have followed Trump in evoking the protests, which have spread to other countries, to rally voters and condemn immigration.

  • Vice President Vance wrote on X, "Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion," sharing a video of a historic town hall reportedly set ablaze by masked protesters, per AFP.
  • "This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country," Vance contended.

Yes, but: Macron, per a translation of his nationwide address over the weekend protests, said the hundreds of thousands of demonstrators had "legitimate demands" and should not be conflated with violent rioters.

  • He said those concerns included the cost of living and fuel price spikes triggered by the war in Iran.

The bottom line: The spiraling violence has created a global shock that Trump is harnessing as a boogeyman ahead of an uphill midterm battle.

Go deeper: Police, protesters clash in Paris as tens of thousands rally across France

item.title: The manosphere stars who helped Trump win are losing their shine
item.description:
The manosphere stars who helped mobilize young men for Donald Trump in 2024 are losing their shine with that very audience.

Why it matters: Trump and Republicans rode a wave of cultural cachet to reach young male voters. Now, the president and some of his most influential online allies are showing signs of losing their grip on that audience ahead of the 2026 midterms.

Driving the news: New polling from the Democratic project Speaking With American Men suggests some of the most prominent influencers during Trump's 2024 campaign have lost their luster with young male voters, per Puck News,

  • Joe Rogan's favorable rating among young men dropped from 11 points, while Elon Musk's popularity dropped 14 points and Tucker Carlson lost 12 points.
  • Andrew Tate, who was arrested on sex trafficking and rape charges, had "a -30 net approval rating," per Puck.

Between the lines: Economic pressures and the Iran war have become major concerns for young men heading into the midterms, Puck reported.

  • Those issues have caused tension between Trump and the influential voices who bolstered his last campaign.

State of play: Young men are turning on politicians, podcasters and influencers, many of whom may have influenced recent political outcomes. They're becoming more skeptical and turning their backs on politicians, especially Trump.

  • The 2026 Young American Men Survey from Cygnal similarly found that among 18- to 30-year-old American men, Trump, Vance and the Republican Party all were viewed unfavorably.
  • Trump's numbers among young voters dropped precipitously. Marquette Law School national polling shows that Trump's approval dropped from 40% in January 2025 to 19% in April 2026, before rebounding to 28% in June. The law school hasn't polled on the question since then.

Yes, but: Young men aren't especially enthusiastic about Democrats, either.

  • Former President Barack Obama, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), and NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani were the only Democrats showing upticks in favorability ratings, per Puck.

Context: Several prominent manosphere personalities have been critical of Trump in his second term, particularly on the Iran war and the Epstein files release.

  • Rogan, like many MAGA influencers, has criticized the war and the Trump administration's handling of the Epstein files.
  • Tucker Carlson has chastised Trump over many issues, including his partnership with Israel in going to war.
  • Vice President Vance has even admitted the White House "screwed up" on its communications about the Epstein files.

Reality check: Researchers question how influential podcasters and personalities actually were in 2024.

  • A September working paper from the NYU Center for Social Media, AI and Politics found that podcast exposure did not necessarily cause Trump's gains among young men.
  • Researchers, who reviewed 36,659 podcast episodes from 2024 alongside two survey datasets, found podcasts explained only a small portion of the widening youth gender gap.

The other side: Influencers still have enormous reach among young voters.

  • A survey from Morning Consult published on Oct. 16 found that nearly two-thirds of Gen Z adults say they get news from creators, while 62% trust creator recommendations.
  • Business Insider reports that one in four U.S. adults feel influencer content has affected their voting decisions.
  • Separate Marquette polling found that 54% of adults who consumed podcasts for political news approved of Trump's job performance in June, compared with 38% of adults overall.

The bottom line: The manosphere's biggest personalities still have sway, but the direction of the country isn't helping them — or Trump — with young men.

item.title: How the energy crisis could become a food security crisis
item.description:
The Iran war and the Ukraine-Russia conflict are creating a "multidirectional squeeze on world agriculture" that could spiral into a crisis, a new report finds.

Why it matters: Wars and extreme weather are colliding to threaten global food supplies and drive up prices, especially in vulnerable economies.

  • The report explores how the El Niño phenomenon could compound the problems of restricted supplies of key fertilizer ingredients, higher fuel costs on the farm and more.
  • The S&P Global Institute report is an unusually holistic look at the topic.

Driving the news: The analysis comes alongside new warnings about food from the International Monetary Fund.

  • Its World Economic Outlook last week sees an overall 10% increase in fertilizer prices this year and food costs rising by 5% in 2026 and 2.4% in 2027, though it depends on the region.
  • "Higher energy and food prices could have severe effects on poverty and food security" and threaten political stability in vulnerable economies, the IMF warned.

State of play: Food producers need steady supplies of natural gas and sulfur for fertilizer, diesel for farm machinery and food transport, and open sea lanes for trade, S&P notes.

  • "Conflict is now testing all of them at once, just as El Niño tests the harvest," states the report from the research and consulting firm.
  • "The risk is increasing, especially for low-income countries, where food costs amount to about half of household spending," it states.

Zoom out: The disruptions could affect agricultural production worldwide, from soybeans and corn in Brazil to wheat in Australia, S&P finds.

The intrigue: The S&P report also warns of something that has received somewhat less attention.

  • The diesel supply crunch doesn't just raise costs for farmers. It also works alongside pro-biofuels policies to make biodiesel production more attractive.
  • "The knock-on effect is that, in some regions, crops for fuel become more valuable than crops for food."

Zoom in: A few stats via S&P illustrate the overlapping threats.

  • Middle Eastern prices for exported sulfur, a fertilizer ingredient, reached a record $1,000 per metric ton in July, after starting the year at a historically high $500 per metric ton.
  • 47% of the global sulfur trade normally goes through the Strait of Hormuz.
  • In Indonesia, industrial use of palm oil, largely for biodiesel, is expected to be roughly five times its 2015-16 level.

The bottom line: A global food crisis is by no means certain.

  • But if wars keep disrupting energy and fertilizer supplies, and weather cuts harvests in key regions, "the elements of such a crisis will be falling into place," S&P warns.

item.title: Trump isn't out to hurt Ukraine, Rubio tells Zelensky
item.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in a phone call Tuesday that President Trump hasn't issued any kind of order to harm Ukraine.

Why it matters: The call was an effort to prevent the crisis between the U.S. and Ukraine from escalating further — and to push back on Ukrainian accusations that Trump is trying to coerce Zelensky into making concessions to Russia.

  • The 45-minute call took place several hours ahead of a new round of peace talks with White House envoy Steve Witkoff aimed at reaching a unified position with European allies on an updated peace proposal to present to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Driving the news: The crisis broke out 10 days ago when Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia at the same time his envoys were in negotiations with Ukrainian officials in Miami.

  • Zelensky on Monday lobbied a bipartisan group of senators to press the Trump administration to remove what he says are restrictions on intelligence sharing and weapons supplies.

Behind the scenes: Rubio told reporters on Tuesday that he clarified to Zelensky that the Pentagon hasn't changed anything when it comes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine, weapons sales or restrictions on the use of the Starshield satellite system.

  • "No change was ordered. It is not true that we restricted it," Rubio said.
  • Rubio acknowledged to Zelensky that there could be a delay in sending Patriot interceptors that have already been paid for by NATO countries. But the reason, he said, is that the U.S. needs to make sure it has enough to protect its own military bases around the world.
  • "Nothing is being deliberately denied. We balance between our obligations to partners and our own needs," he said. "There hasn't been a deliberate political directive to harm Ukraine."
  • Rubio also asserted that the several cases in which Ukraine didn't get advance warning of Russian ballistic missile attacks were a result of technical failures, not a U.S. order.

What he's saying: "No doubt there are tensions," he said. "That is why we had the call. The president is frustrated. The president is responding to the insinuation that he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine, which is not fair and not true."

  • Rubio said Trump is "angry and frustrated" about the lack of progress in peace talks between Russia and Ukraine after two years of efforts.

The other side: Zelensky wrote on X after the call that he is "grateful" for Rubio's "readiness to help and his clear position."

  • He said Ukraine needs ballistic missile interceptors and early warnings to protect Ukrainian citizens and stressed that "the situation with Starlink and Starshield needs to be restored."

State of play: Witkoff arrived in Oslo on Tuesday for talks with Zelensky and European leaders.

  • The talks there are expected to include Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, President of Finland Alexander Stubb, representatives of the E4 nations (the U.K., France, Germany and Poland) and officials from the EU and NATO.
  • Following Oslo, Witkoff plans to travel to Russia to meet with Putin and present ideas developed in consultation with Ukrainian and European leaders.

item.title: AI takes on great experiment in self-rule
item.description:
Slowly but surely, the leading AI companies are creating a national self-governing structure to oversee their technology and its societal impact.

  • With the federal government largely hands-off, Anthropic, OpenAI and others are self-regulating their technology and now setting up their own plans to redistribute their wealth.

Why it matters: Not since the age of the robber barons have America's industrial titans wielded such sweeping power to shape society — and decide how their private fortunes should serve the public good.

  • In the modern era, Washington has largely exercised those powers through regulation, taxation and public spending.

The big picture: President Trump has no interest in new regulations. Instead, he has blessed a basic framework for the AI companies to regulate themselves — and potentially each other — outside of formal government monitoring.

  • Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Elon Musk's XSI, Meta and Nvidia are working on different versions of this. This is all voluntary and rests on the public trusting companies the size of industrialized nations to responsibly police themselves.
  • These companies are in a frantic race to create human-surpassing superintelligence. All are pressing ahead, even as their leaders — particularly at Anthropic — warn of potentially catastrophic risks and profound economic disruption.
  • At the same time, some AI leaders are promising to direct a portion of their vast wealth to benefit those outside their companies.

Zoom in: At least three competing visions are emerging for sharing the spoils of the AI boom, each with a different answer to who should control the wealth.

  • Anthropic: The company. On the eve of its blockbuster IPO, Anthropic pledged 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund that could grow into one of the largest philanthropic institutions in history. At a hypothetical $2 trillion valuation, its stake would be worth $100 billion — more than the Gates Foundation's current endowment. Including earlier founder and employee pledges, roughly 20% of Anthropic's shares are earmarked for the public good.
  • Musk: The people. Musk responded to Anthropic's announcement by urging the company to give shares "directly to the public." On Monday, Musk pledged to give every American child a share of SpaceX next year — a staggering $10.5 billion giveaway at current prices. Musk called it the "first of many," though he offered no details on how the unprecedented distribution would work.
  • OpenAI: The government. CEO Sam Altman has floated giving the U.S. government a 5% stake in OpenAI through a sovereign wealth fund — potentially handing Washington a multibillion-dollar interest in one of the world's most powerful AI companies. Altman envisions an Alaska-style fund that could distribute the industry's investment returns directly to Americans, though the plan remains preliminary and would likely require congressional approval.

Reality check: The numbers are staggering. So are the assumptions about future wealth, billionaire follow-through and the public's willingness to trust its benefactors.

  • Bill Gates and Warren Buffett launched the Giving Pledge in 2010, a voluntary promise by billionaires — including Musk — to give away most of their fortunes. Gates built a philanthropic empire, only to become a lightning rod for conspiracy theories.
  • Anthropic's ambitions depend on extraordinary growth projections — its own employees envision 17% GDP growth in 2030 — while Musk has a history of making spectacular promises that fail to materialize.
  • Anthropic's roots in effective altruism, a philosophy deeply distrusted by the Trump administration and its allies, also raise a more fundamental question: Who gets to define the public good?

Between the lines: No industry requirements or consensus exist on how best to redistribute their expected wealth. But Trump Accounts — which allow families, businesses and individuals to invest in tax-advantaged funds for children — are emerging as a favorite vehicle for free-market AI leaders.

  • Billionaire investor Brad Gerstner, a driving force behind the program, is championing a vision of broad-based ownership in which ordinary Americans share directly in the economic upside of the AI revolution.
  • SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband in July pledged roughly $320 million in company shares to 2 million children through Trump Accounts — a potential blueprint for distributing an even larger slice of Musk's fortune.

What to watch: The Trump administration hasn't fully relinquished its regulatory authority, potentially complicating the emerging experiment in AI self-governance.

  • After Anthropic disclosed that its AI had submitted a false homicide tip to Philadelphia police and improperly interacted with government websites, the White House declared that AI companies must report security incidents and remedy any harm.
  • "This notification and remediation process is not optional," Trump's Super Intelligence Force warned — a striking assertion of federal authority just weeks after the president blessed a voluntary system of industry oversight.

Axios' Zachary Basu and Bradley Olson contributed reporting.

item.title: Empathy divides Americans by religion, with white evangelicals standing apart
item.description:
Data: PRRI, 2026 American Values Survey; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios

White evangelical Protestants are the only major religious group in which a majority says empathy can become dangerous when it leads people away from a society guided by God's truth, according to a new survey.

Why it matters: The survey lands amid a quiet civil war within American Christianity over who deserves empathy.

  • Conservatives ranging from evangelical pastors to Elon Musk have framed empathy as a vulnerability in debates over immigration, racial justice and LGBTQ+ rights.
  • In a February 2025 interview with Joe Rogan, Musk called empathy "the fundamental weakness of Western civilization," while acknowledging its potential good and warning against its weaponization.

By the numbers: The annual American Values Survey from the nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute (PRRI) released Tuesday found that 42% of white evangelical Protestants agreed that empathy is a foundational moral value that helps build a healthy society.

  • Separately, 54% agreed that empathy can become dangerous when it leads people away from a society guided by God's truth.
  • In every other religious group, PRRI found that at least 66% agreed with the foundational-value statement, including 73% of white mainline Protestants and Hispanic Catholics.
  • Empathy's foundational value was endorsed by 83% of religiously unaffiliated Americans, 80% of respondents grouped under other non-Christian religions, 77% of Jewish Americans and 65% of Latter-day Saints.

The intrigue: The survey found a 30-point partisan gap: 84% of Democrats agreed with the foundational-value statement, compared with 54% of Republicans. Independents were at 70%.

  • White evangelicals stand out among religious groups, but PRRI reports religious and partisan results separately.
  • The survey doesn't establish how much white evangelicals contribute to the Republican-Democratic gap.

Zoom in: The divide also tracks with PRRI's Christian nationalism measure. Among people PRRI classifies as Christian nationalism adherents, 38% agreed that empathy is foundational, compared with 94% of rejecters.

  • PRRI classifies respondents as Christian nationalist adherents or sympathizers based on support for a U.S. government and laws grounded in Christianity and the view that Christians should exercise dominion over society.
  • Six in 10 adherents agreed that empathy can become dangerous, compared with 6% of rejecters.

What they're saying: "As Christian nationalist leaders attack the sentiment of empathy, a disturbing 'empathy gap' has opened, separating Republicans and white evangelicals from most other Americans," PRRI President and Founder Robert P. Jones said in a statement.

  • Jones said the findings raise questions about the moral foundations that let people from different backgrounds share a democracy.

Methodology: PRRI conducted the American Values Survey online Aug. 20–Sept. 7, 2026, among 5,200 adults in Ipsos' KnowledgePanel and 339 additional adults recruited through opt-in panels to increase sample sizes in smaller states. The survey covered adults ages 18 and older in all 50 states and the District of Columbia.

  • The margin of sampling error is ±1.6 percentage points at the 95% confidence level for results based on the entire sample.
